#5456. Measles update: First death in Virginia, ninth in Pennsylvania

Measles update: First death in Virginia, ninth in Pennsylvania" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Virginia Department of Health announced on Nov. 20 its first measles-associated death since 1978.

It is the fourth state this year to have reported a measles-associated death, following Pennsylvania, where a ninth death was reported on Monday, as well as New York and Wisconsin. Pennsylvania's health department said it has now confirmed 1,638 cases across 46 of its counties this year, and noted that only five of those were among individuals vaccinated against the disease.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as of a Nov. 19 update, lists 5,838 confirmed cases of measles this year, well above 2025's total of 2,289. The agency has recognized six of the reported deaths as compared to states' 13, as the federal body said it is looking to develop a standardized definition for deaths due to measles amid disputes over the use and reporting of "measles-associated" deaths.

The United States has lost its measles elimination status, and has now exceeded 5,400 cases and 10 total measles-associated deaths in 2026.

The status determination from the Pan American Health Organization, which is part of the World Health Organization, was made late last week and first reported by the Wall Street Journal before being confirmed by other outlets. (Editor's note: The public health body made its official announcement on Nov. 17)

The U.S. had notched elimination status, reflecting no continuous spread of the disease for at least 12 months, in 2000. Regaining it similarly requires the country to stop continuous spread for 12 months. PAHO recommends countries that have lost elimination status submit and enact a corrective action plan that includes immunization and surveillance.

The decision landed shortly after the country hit 5,412 confirmed measles cases, per a Nov. 13 update from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The federal public health body also lists 591 hospitalizations (11% rate) and six deaths—though it has been hesitant to outright confirm states' reports of measles-associated deaths, of which there have now been 10.

Health groups and public health professionals have pointed to lagging vaccination rates and checked endorsement of routine childhood vaccines from current leadership at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, namely Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., as fueling the country's outbreaks.

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services on Thursday reported its first measles-outbreak associated death since 1990.

The deceased was an infant whose case was among many in the southwestern part of the state, for whom the coroner listed measles as immediate cause of death. As of Nov. 3, the department has reported 431 cases across 13 counties in 2026, the highest number of cases in over 35 years. All but three of those are among individuals who were not vaccinated, and nine have involved hospitalizations.

"Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, said in the announcement. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family."

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

The New York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

The state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

Sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department said. Many of New York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

In a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease."

"This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told Fierce Healthcare that it had deployed epidemiologists and other experts to New York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is currently scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they said.

Of the roughly $100 million in additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to New York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they said.

"Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

The U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

The vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a new, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

The CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and new CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not launched the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

#5454. Centralized platform for submitting, managing out-of-network billing disputes launches

Centralized platform for submitting, managing out-of-network billing disputes launches" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has launched a new online portal for payers, providers and other stakeholders to manage and monitor disputes under the federal Independent Dispute Resolution process.

The IDR Gateway went online Nov. 13 and was officially unveiled Nov. 20. It replaces the web forms parties previously used to manage disputes, most of which will no longer be available outside of the centralized platform after Jan. 15, 2027, per a government fact sheet.

Payers will eventually be required to register on IDR Gateway so that it is easier for providers to identify the correct party, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said earlier this year when finalizing an overhaul of No Surprises Act protocols. That registration feature will be added “in the future on a rolling basis,” CMS said last week, with others like in-portal negotiation similarly rolling out over time “to improve accountability and reduce unnecessary filings,” the agency said last spring.

For now, the IDR Gateway allows parties and their representatives to initiate a dispute, respond to proposed selections of IDR entities and submit a payment offer. Its other tools allow users to view, search, set up notifications and broadly analyze open disputes for their organization; an IDR Gateway Dashboard, CMS said, offers a color-coded donut chart breaking down an organization’s different types of open disputes by phase, while another tool can generate detailed reports of dispute line items.

The administration also touted security measures inherent to the new portal. These include a new sign-up process that requires users to verify their identity with an approved credential service provider, and other protocols like a terms and conditions agreement that notes that unauthorized users could be subject to criminal prosecution.

The baseball-style IDR process enacted under the No Surprises Act, intended to handle out-of-network billing disputes away from the patient’s purview, has become a point of contention amid dispute volumes and payouts well beyond legislators’ expectations.

Arbitrators’ decisions have largely favored providers over payers (85% of decisions went toward providers last year), which alongside court decisions that tweaked CMS’ processes further toward provider preferences, has triggered outright condemnation from payers who have turned to lawsuits, restrictive policies and lobbying in a bit to reform the process. Recent analyses have pegged the IDR process’ impact for employer plans at $8.4 billion in 2025 and total costs associated with the process at $22 billion for that same year.

Lawmakers including the No Surprises Act’s chief authors have said they hope to pass new legislation to fix or fully replace the IDR process, with December’s must-pass budget bill now looking like a likely vehicle for such a change.

#5453. Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits. Although heavy drinking was linked to worse health outcomes regardless of the beverage, the picture was more complicated among people who consumed smaller amounts of alcohol.

Researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease. In contrast, similar amounts of beer, cider, and spirits were linked to a higher risk. The findings, presented at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session (ACC.26), suggest that both the type and quantity of alcohol may influence its relationship with long-term health.

The results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health. Importantly, the new findings do not establish that wine itself protects against disease.

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," said Zhangling Chen, MD, PhD, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author.

How a Study of 340,000 Adults Measured Alcohol Risk

To investigate the relationship between drinking habits and longevity, scientists examined data from 340,924 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2022. The UK Biobank is a large research resource that collects health and lifestyle information to help scientists investigate factors associated with disease and mortality.

Participants reported their alcohol consumption through dietary questionnaires when they joined the study. Researchers then classified them into four groups based on how much pure alcohol they typically consumed each day or week, rather than simply counting drinks.

This distinction matters because beer, wine, and spirits contain different concentrations of alcohol. For comparison, a 12-ounce can of beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits each provide approximately 14 grams of pure alcohol.

People consuming fewer than 20 g (about 1.5 standard drinks) per week were placed in the never or occasional drinking group. Low consumption was defined as 20 g per week up to 20 g per day for men, and 20 g per week up to 10 g per day for women.

Moderate drinking was defined as 20 g to 40 g (about 1.5 to three standard drinks) daily for men and 10 g to 20 g daily for women. High consumption meant more than 40 g (about three drinks) per day for men or more than 20 g (about 1.5 drinks) per day for women.

Researchers followed participants' health outcomes for an average of more than 13 years, allowing them to examine how drinking patterns were associated with deaths from different causes.

Wine, Beer, and Spirits Show Different Heart Health Risks

The clearest finding concerned heavy alcohol consumption. Compared with people who never drank or consumed alcohol only occasionally, heavy drinkers had a 24% higher risk of dying from any cause. Their risk of dying from cancer was 36% higher, while their risk of dying from heart disease was 14% higher.

These increased risks were associated with heavy drinking regardless of whether participants preferred wine, beer, cider, or spirits.

However, the results became more surprising when researchers examined low and moderate alcohol consumption. At these levels, the type of beverage was associated with substantially different outcomes.

People who consumed wine in low to moderate amounts had a significantly lower risk of death, while those who consumed comparable amounts of beer, cider, or spirits had a significantly higher risk.

The contrast was especially striking for cardiovascular disease, a broad category of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than people who never or only occasionally drank alcohol.

By comparison, even low consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was associated with a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.

These percentages describe relative differences in risk between groups, not the absolute probability that an individual will die from cardiovascular disease. Because the research was observational, the findings also cannot demonstrate that choosing one alcoholic beverage over another directly changes a person's risk.

"Our findings help clarify previously mixed evidence on low to moderate alcohol consumption," Chen said. "These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed, but also on the type of beverage. Even low to moderate intake of spirits, beer, or cider is linked to higher mortality, while low to moderate intake of wine may carry lower risk."

Why Might Wine Be Linked to Lower Heart Risks?

Researchers identified several possible explanations for the differences, including the chemical composition of wine and the habits of people who drink it.

Red wine contains polyphenols, naturally occurring compounds found in plants that can have antioxidant properties. Antioxidants help counter certain chemical reactions involving unstable molecules that can damage cells. Some polyphenols have been investigated for potential benefits to blood vessels and cardiovascular function.

These compounds could contribute to the associations observed in wine drinkers, although the study did not establish that they were responsible for the lower mortality risk.

Another possible explanation involves how and when people drink.

Wine is more commonly consumed alongside meals, and wine drinkers often report healthier diets and lifestyle habits. Drinking wine may therefore be associated with other behaviors that support cardiovascular health.

Beer, cider, and spirits, on the other hand, are more frequently consumed outside of meals. In this study, people who favored these beverages also tended to have poorer overall diet quality and other lifestyle factors associated with increased health risks.

Such differences make it difficult to separate the effects of the alcohol itself from the characteristics and habits of the people consuming it.

"Taken together, these factors suggest that the type of alcohol, how it is consumed, and the associated lifestyle behaviors all contribute to the observed differences in mortality risk," Chen said.

What the Findings Mean for Alcohol and Health

To make their comparisons more reliable, the researchers statistically adjusted their analyses for numerous factors that might influence mortality. These included age and other demographic characteristics, socioeconomic circumstances, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic health.

Cardiometabolic factors include conditions and measurements related to heart and metabolic health, such as blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, and cholesterol levels. The analyses also accounted for family histories of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Even with these adjustments, the researchers emphasized several important limitations.

Because the study was observational, it could identify associations between alcohol consumption and mortality but could not prove that particular beverages caused better or worse outcomes. Other differences between participants may have influenced the findings despite the statistical adjustments.

Alcohol intake was also measured through questionnaires completed when participants first entered the study. That information depended on participants accurately reporting their own drinking habits, and it did not capture changes in consumption during the years that followed.

Another consideration is that UK Biobank participants tend to be healthier than the general population. This could limit how well the findings apply to other groups of people.

The researchers suggested that high-quality randomized trials could provide stronger evidence about the health effects of different drinking patterns. Such studies would help clarify whether the observed differences reflect the beverages themselves or other factors associated with their consumption.

Nevertheless, the enormous study population and more than 13 years of average follow-up provide considerable statistical strength. By examining specific types of alcohol, different levels of consumption, and multiple causes of death, the research offers a more detailed picture of alcohol's potential health risks than many earlier investigations.

The findings highlight an important distinction: while heavy drinking is consistently associated with harmful health outcomes, the relationships observed at lower consumption levels may depend on beverage choice, drinking habits, and broader lifestyle patterns.

For now, the apparent advantage among wine drinkers should not be interpreted as a reason to start drinking wine for heart health. The evidence points to a complex relationship between alcohol and mortality, rather than proving that any alcoholic drink offers protection.

Ziyue Li presented the study, "Alcohol Use at Mid-Life and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality," at ACC.26.

WASHINGTON — A new website launched by the Trump administration provides centralized access to more than 92,000 public records from the Department of Health and Human Services and the agencies it oversees — including partially redacted entries from health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s calendar.While many of the records were previously available, the health department heralded the launch of the site as a sign of its “radical transparency.”

In June, after a New York Times report referred to him as disengaged with the job, Kennedy said on social media that his calendar was publicly available, though no such calendar had been made available for the media or the public before Tuesday. A number of Freedom of Information Act requests filed by STAT reporters had previously gone unanswered and even unacknowledged and do not appear to be included in the Tuesday release.

Much of the secretary’s partial calendar, which reflects his activities from Feb. 13, 2025, to June 19, 2026, is redacted, including some private calls taken by the secretary. One of his closest aides at the agency, Stefanie Spear, appears to be listed only once in the calendar. References to other notable meetings are not redacted, including one that would ultimately lead to the ouster of a short-lived director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Susan Monarez.

#5451. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT

Intelligent data infrastructure is becoming a priority as enterprises move artificial intelligence beyond isolated pilots and into production environments.

The shift places new demands on storage systems built to support traditional applications, especially as organizations introduce AI workloads across hybrid and multicloud environments. NetApp Inc. is responding with a strategy that emphasizes infrastructure modernization without requiring enterprises to abandon existing investments, according to George Kurian (pictured), chief executive officer of NetApp.

“I think that the AI era requires organizations to be really good stewards of their data, because data is the foundation for knowledge and knowledge is the intellectual property,” he told theCUBE. “To have knowledge, you need really good intelligent data infrastructure that not only allows you to extract memory and context from your data, but also to keep it secure, well governed and a resource that you can trust.”

Kurian spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand and co-host Rebecca Knight during NetApp INSIGHT, in an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The event’s coverage featured NetApp executives and technology partners discussing the evolving demands on enterprise data infrastructure and the challenges of bringing AI into production. (Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with George Kurian:

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT:

Enterprise AI workloads are exposing limitations in storage architectures designed for more predictable application demands. NetApp’s Novus architecture separates data and metadata management so each can scale independently. The company’s AI Data Engine is designed to discover, classify and prepare enterprise data for AI applications, according to Syam Nair, chief product officer of NetApp.

“Performance and throughput of accessing the data, that’s a necessity for AI, but that won’t be sufficient for agents to actually act on the data,” he said during the event. “If the data is not ready and it’s not protected, you get fast results. You get compromised results, but they may not be the ones you want.”

The demands of AI factories are also changing how storage resources must be managed. NetApp’s approach aims to support high-throughput AI pipelines without sacrificing the responsiveness other applications require, according to Arindam Banerjee, chief platform and technology officer of NetApp, who spoke alongside Jason Hardy, vice president of storage technology at Nvidia Corp.

“What happens is [that] different types of workloads like transactional workloads for metadata and heavy sequential workloads for, say, checkpoints, happen at the same time,” Banerjee told theCUBE. “Previous architectures did one or the other very well. They never were able to combine it and do both at the same time.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jason Hardy and Arindam Banerjee:

Modernizing enterprise infrastructure often requires organizations to accommodate existing applications while introducing new AI capabilities. NetApp and Oracle Corp. are addressing that challenge through a co-engineered, fully managed storage service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

“When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”

NetApp and Oracle Corp. are extending enterprise storage capabilities into the public cloud through a co-engineered, fully managed service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

“When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”

The integration challenge extends beyond cloud storage to the networking and compute resources that support AI workloads. NetApp and Cisco Systems Inc. are expanding their FlexPod infrastructure with validated designs intended to reduce deployment complexity. The partnership has served 10,000 customers over 16 years, according to James Cole, vice president of data center networking, business development, partnerships and go-to-market at Cisco, and Alvaro Celis, chief partner and ecosystem officer at NetApp.

“Twenty years ago, 10 years ago, you would’ve been designing your data structures and your applications around the infrastructure. Now we’ve turned that on its head,” Cole said during the event. “You’re really designing the infrastructure around the movement of data. Who better to do that together than the person you trust with your data and the person you trust with your network?”

Another partnership focuses on private AI deployment and measurable business outcomes. The NetApp AIPod Mini combines NetApp infrastructure with the Generate platform from Iterate Studio Inc., doing business as Iterate.ai, according to Brian Sathianathan, co-founder and chief technology officer of Iterate.ai. In one insurance deployment cited during the discussion, an agent reduced accident-report analysis from approximately eight hours to eight minutes.

“AIPod Mini has attached connections to the NetApp storage, and it talks to NetApp using the ONTAP protocol that’s time-tested,” he said during the event. “Then, on top of the AIPod Mini, we are running our Generate software. That software has a [large language model] embedded in it, so you can run all your AI queries locally and fully privately within your four walls.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Alvaro Celis and James Cole:

As enterprises introduce autonomous agents into infrastructure management, intelligent data infrastructure must accommodate increasingly complex operational demands. NetApp’s unified control plane, delivered through NetApp Console, is designed to reduce routine administrative work through policy-driven automation. In one keynote demonstration, agents responded to a nighttime performance anomaly, according to Sandeep Singh, senior vice president and general manager of enterprise storage at NetApp.

“Agents can, in real time, implement the necessary quality of service rules to ensure there’s compliance to the boundary conditions there,” he told theCUBE. “And that way, no human is woken up. The right outcome is achieved, and there’s no noisy neighbor effect. And there’s an audit trail presented to the humans for going and following up.”

Automation, however, can’t resolve organizational questions about data ownership and responsibility. As enterprises extend intelligent data infrastructure across applications and environments, leadership must establish accountability for the information those systems rely on, according to Helen Yu, founder and chief executive officer of Tigon Advisory Corp., who appeared alongside Singh.

“It’s not a storage problem. It’s a leadership and accountability issue,” she said during the event. “When teams don’t have access to … trusted data consistently, they actually stop making decisions. They start making workarounds.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Helen Yu and Sandeep Singh:

#5450. Academic hospital heads petition Congress for 2-year delay to CMS' 340B cuts

Academic hospital heads petition Congress for 2-year delay to CMS' 340B cuts" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Dozens of academic health system and teaching hospital chief executives are turning to Congress in a bid to blunt a controversial subsidy cut coming to Medicare Part B in the new year.

Earlier this month, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services locked in plans to reduce reimbursements for outpatient drugs dispensed by participants in the 340B Drug Pricing Program during the 2027 calendar year.

Specifically, the agency said it will move from the current rate of average sales price (ASP) plus 6% down to ASP minus 28%, with a corresponding 7.5% increase in non-drug outpatient payments to maintain budget neutrality. CMS said the change will reduce Original Medicare drug payments by an estimated $4.35 billion and drug payments from beneficiaries by $1.1 billion during the policy’s first year.

Hospital groups—particularly those that chiefly represent nonprofit or safety-net hospitals—have denounced the plan’s disproportionate effect on hospitals participating in the decades-old subsidy program, as well as a gift to for-profit hospitals that do not participate but will benefit from the budget-neutral offset.

With their formal opposition to the policy’s proposal set aside by CMS, 95 executives whose organizations are members of the Association of American Medical Colleges have now penned a letter to leaders of the House and the Senate pleading for a two-year delay to the rate cut’s implementation.

“This policy will exacerbate already negative Medicare margins at a time when teaching hospitals are already grappling with rising financial challenges resulting from inflation, workforce shortages, manufacturer-driven restrictions on the 340B program and an expected rise in uncompensated care costs,” they wrote.

The executives acknowledged that the final policy’s rate of ASP minus 28% is “slightly smaller” than CMS’ initial proposal of ASP minus 33.4%, but said the change was still a threat to the country’s healthcare safety net. They noted the cuts represent a nearly $5.5 billion reduction that would be disproportionately shouldered by AAMC-member teaching hospitals—who comprise 17% of all impacted hospitals—but will see almost $3 billion of that total.

Those funds are necessary to finance critical care services at academic hospitals including trauma care, inpatient behavioral care, transplant surgery and labor and delivery, the signatories warned lawmakers. They also noted that their institutions are major referral hubs that accept “the most complex transfer cases from lower acuity settings, such as rural and community hospitals,” in a way that for-profit hospitals and others who will benefit from the final rule do not.

“While we understand that Congress has an interest in improving the 340B program, and are broadly supportive of meaningful transparency and accountability for covered entities, we also strongly believe that cutting Medicare payment to 340B hospitals is not the appropriate policy mechanism to achieve these goals,” they wrote. “Therefore, we respectfully request that you support a two-year delay in the [Outpatient Prospective Payment System] rule’s payment cuts for 340B-acquired drugs.”

Among the letter’s 95 signatories were the heads of Cedars-Sinai, Stanford Health Care, Yale New Haven Health, Tampa General Hospital, Rush University System for Health, Mass General Brigham, Nebraska Medicine, RWJBarnabas Health, NewYork-Presbyterian, UNC Health and School of Medicine, OHSU, Jefferson Health, Penn Medicine, Vanderbilt Health and Froedtert ThedaCare.

The academic health systems and hospitals’ turn to lawmakers comes after their rebukes of CMS’ 340B policy have fallen on deaf ears. The agency and broader Trump administration have often sided with critics of the subsidy program on related initiatives like a pilot rebate program, citing 340B’s rapid growth and contribution to increased healthcare spending. A Health and Human Services Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation policy brief defending the rate cut made those views crystal clear with claims that the program has incentivized provider consolidation while doing little to serve patients’ needs.

Meanwhile, Congress, spurred by public pressure to reduce healthcare costs, has proposed its own legislative fixes to 340B. Though each bill aims to preserve the program and subsidize safety-net care, some are more friendly to the hospital industry than others.

#5449. Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

As marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering important questions about its effects on mental health. A major new study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.

Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.

The findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.

"What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," said lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an important mental health concern that deserves attention."

Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link

The connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults showed particularly elevated risks.

Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.

The consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.

Yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.

"Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood."

The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.

The study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.

This distinction is important because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.

The findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.

Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.

Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening

One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.

Rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.

"Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," said Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support."

The study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.

However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.

The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an important role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.

As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.

Said Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked."

Materials provided by Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs. Original written by W.B. Kagan. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5448. Despite stalling in court, Trump restrictions on foreign students have had a chilling effect on enrollment

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

West Coast Biotech & Life Sciences Reporter

Jonathan Wosen is STAT’s West Coast biotech & life sciences reporter. You can reach Jonathan on Signal at jwosen.27.

Even as judges have blocked visa restrictions and other limits on foreign scholars and scientists, the Trump administration is winning outside court. New data show a clear drop in the enrollment of international graduate students, a key piece of the U.S. biomedical workforce.

That paradox was on full display last week. On Nov. 16, a federal judge issued a final ruling blocking a proposed four-year cap on how long international students and postdoctoral researchers can remain in the country. The next day, a judge in a separate case issued a preliminary injunction preventing the administration from narrowing eligibility for a work authorization program widely used by foreign students.

To student advocates like Fanta Aw, CEO of the nonprofit NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the rulings represented two wins in two days. “I’ve always believed that our judicial systems are strong and are very much still in play, and I felt relieved,” said Aw, whose organization is a plaintiff in both cases. “Our members, and in particular our students, I felt, were vindicated.”

But data released the same day as the ruling in the visa time limit case paint a less celebratory picture. A survey of more than 800 U.S. institutions conducted by the Institute of International Education found that foreign student enrollment for the current academic year has decreased 9% overall compared with 2025, with a 15% drop among newly enrolled students and graduate students. While IIE won’t have complete data until next year, the preliminary numbers suggest this will be the third consecutive year graduate enrollment has dropped — with the largest year-to-year decrease in at least 20 years, according to historical data from the nonprofit.

That trend extends to biomedicine, where foreign students make up nearly a quarter of life science Ph.D. graduates, according to new survey data from the Association of American Medical Colleges. A poll of 37 AAMC member institutions showed that the number of international students starting biomedical Ph.D. programs has decreased by about 30% since 2024, more than twice the 14% overall decline in matriculation in these programs.

The growing body of data as well as STAT’s interviews with students and immigration experts suggest that, despite the legal losses, the Trump administration’s policies on immigration have had a chilling effect on students considering coming to the U.S., and on those who are already here. Meanwhile, enrollment of foreign students is rising at some Asian universities, and experts warn that these opposing trends could jeopardize the nation’s biomedical preeminence and that it could take years to repair the loss of trust from students who no longer see the U.S. as a welcoming destination.

“People are looking at us from overseas, going, ‘We don’t really recognize this country,’” said Elizabeth Goss, an immigration attorney based in Boston. Even if Democrats’ new majority in Congress prevents further restrictions, she added, “I think we have a lot of ground to make up.”

When contacted for comment, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson wrote in an email that the agency’s records don’t support the decline reported by IIE, though it didn’t say whether its own data show lower enrollment by foreign students, and that President Trump should be credited for cracking down on rampant visa fraud.

“Institute of International Education’s ‘reporting’ is completely misleading and not backed up by any real evidence,” the DHS spokesperson said. “So far, [the Student and Exchange Visitor Program] has not experienced a 9% drop of foreign student enrollment.”

A recent independent analysis by the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration  of the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System, a DHS database that has for more than 20 years monitored foreign students, found that international student enrollment declined by 6.3% between October 2025 and October 2026.

Concerns that the Trump administration would make it difficult for foreign scientists to enter or stay in the U.S. preceded the president’s inauguration. Since then, the administration has enacted travel bans affecting dozens of countries; instituted “extreme vetting” for visa applicants, including the review of social media profiles; and revoked more than 8,000 student visas. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has also stepped up enforcement of alleged visa violations, including the recent detention of a Princeton neuroscience Ph.D. student who had been traveling home after presenting at a scientific meeting.

But many of the administration’s efforts to more tightly regulate international scholars have not come to fruition. That includes the attempt to end “duration of status,” a policy that for nearly half a century allowed students and postdoctoral researchers to stay in the U.S. for the length of their training. DHS’s proposed four-year cap would likely have forced the vast majority of new foreign life science students to apply for extensions to stay in the country given that, on average, it takes five to six years to earn a biomedical doctorate. But a federal judge found that the proposal violated the Administrative Procedure Act, a law that governs how agencies implement new regulations.

The Trump administration has also proposed a $70,000 fee for a popular work authorization program meant to give students professional experience; academic institutions would be expected to pay the fee. And DHS is attempting to revive plans to institute a $100,000 fee for H1-B visas, which are often used by foreign workers in high-skill fields such as biotech.

Even though these restrictions have not been enacted, they’ve left many foreign students with a clear sense that they aren’t wanted here.

“All these rules, it just made me feel like my immigration was a crime. That’s the biggest recurring feeling that I’ve had these past few years,” said a biomedical Ph.D. student at the University of Washington, who requested anonymity to speak freely. “You know what? I’m just here to study. I’m just learning, and I’m focused on my science. But it has felt very disruptive.”

There are growing signs that fear is impacting student decisions. A poll this summer from the Association of American Universities found that, while domestic student applications for U.S. Ph.D. programs went up by 3% this year, international applications fell 21%.

A more recent survey of 437 universities, including more than 200 in the U.S., found that nearly 60% of U.S. institutions reported lower graduate enrollment between August and October compared with the same period last year. Ninety percent of U.S. respondents cited restrictive government policies as a significant obstacle.

That trend isn’t unique to the U.S. The Global Enrollment Benchmark Survey found that nearly 80% of institutions in the United Kingdom, which has also instituted tougher immigration controls, reported reduced foreign graduate student enrollment. By contrast, nearly 60% of Asian universities that responded, including five Chinese institutions, said graduate enrollment had increased. It’s a shift that Aw says could have major implications for the global economy and the future of innovation.

“There is truly a global competition for talent,” she said. “China has made no secret that one of its most pressing priorities is international education and to bring as many talented students to its shores as they can from around the world. That used to be the United States.”

#5447. Voters expect lawmakers to address healthcare affordability, access: poll

Voters expect lawmakers to address healthcare affordability, access: poll" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Half of voters said they are paying more this year in premiums and out-of-pocket costs, according to a new national poll.

Lake Research Partners and Bellwether Research & Consulting surveyed 1,000 voters between Oct. 20 and Oct. 28 on behalf of the National Health Council, and 50% said their premiums and out-of-pocket costs are higher this year compared to last year. Among those with commercial insurance, 63% said their premiums have risen, and 60% said their out-of-pocket costs have grown year-over-year.

In addition, 25% of those surveyed said they had a claim for a prescription denied, and 24% said they waited more than two weeks for a prior authorization decision. Twenty-one percent said that they struggled to find a specialist.

Healthcare costs and the broader economy were major factors in Democrats' significant victories in the latest midterm election. And the NHC poll finds that voters expect Congress to act on addressing the costs that they face.

Most of the surveyed voters (78%) said they believe that the healthcare system warrants major changes or a complete overhaul, and 84% said they would support a candidate that would make it a priority to reform the healthcare insurance system.

However, 74% of those surveyed rated the effort from elected officials to address affordability and access as either fair or poor.

“Holding onto a plan isn’t the same as being protected by it. Patients are watching their costs rise and their coverage change, and they’re worried about what that means for their families down the road,” said Randall Rutta, CEO of the National Health Council, in an announcement. “The new Congress has a real opportunity to change that, and patients across the country will be watching.”

The survey highlights a number of potential policies that would have broad voter support. For example, 91% of those surveyed said they would support eliminating surprise medical bills and policies to require price transparency.

In addition, 90% said they would back efforts to reduce out-of-pocket costs, while 89% said they favor requiring health plans to cover treatments that were prescribed by doctors. Eighty-eight percent support efforts to increase screening and early detection for medical risks.

"Voters aren't asking lawmakers to talk about health care differently," said Christine Matthews, president of Bellwether Research and Consulting, in the release. "They want to see it work differently. Reform is a priority they expect the new Congress to deliver on."

#5446. Opinion: Washington and Beijing are building walls around biotechnology. That’s the wrong approach

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Kinch is a professor of pharmacology at Stony Brook University and the author of six books on pharmaceutical innovation.

For more than a decade, my colleagues and I at the Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology have tracked every experimental medicine that enters human testing anywhere in the world. Last December, I wrote in STAT that China had reached parity with the United States in terms of the absolute number of new drugs introduced into clinical trials each year. Starting in 2018, the rate of U.S. contributions began to stagnate. Meanwhile, in 2013, Chinese organizations had introduced about 30 new experimental drugs. A decade later, the number topped 400. And there is no reason to expect the momentum in either country is changing.

Over the past month, both governments have seemingly been moving to wall themselves off. On Oct. 16, Beijing proposed barring foreign acquisition of its companies’ proprietary cell and gene platforms. Within a week, the U.S. Department of the Treasury proposed restrictions that would bar Americans from taking equity stakes, forming joint ventures, or making limited-partner investments in Chinese biotech companies and their equipment suppliers.

The proposals from Beijing and Washington do not impact licensing. American drugmakers can keep licensing Chinese molecules, and Chinese companies may develop new medicines to sell to the U.S. and European companies.

That open door matters more than either wall. Data show that the U.S.-China contest in biotechnology is not one race but several. Restricting investment will not help America win the races it is already losing. The bigger threat to U.S. leadership is not Chinese capital. It is the erosion, at home, of the research enterprise that built America’s lead.

The Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology’s newest analysis, published in September in Drug Discovery Today, emphasizes the importance of these continued engagements. My colleagues and I evaluated the 17,000 new drugs that first entered human trials between 2000 and 2024, separating them into eight different modalities. These ranged from conventional pills to gene therapies. The convergence in the numbers of overall active ingredients that we reported last year turned out to be anything but uniform when looking at the details.

The growth by China was concentrated in a key subset of biologics. By the late 2010s, Chinese sponsors often had introduced more, and more novel, cell therapies annually than American sponsors. By the early 2020s, China had matched or exceeded the U.S. in the introduction of new monoclonal antibodies, a commercially important class of biologic drugs. China took a commanding lead in certain categories of monoclonals, such as multispecific antibodies and drug conjugates.

The U.S. still holds a larger share in two categories: nucleic acid drugs and gene therapy. Dominance in both technologies reflects tools built over decades of Western public and private investment. Examples include lipid nanoparticles that conveyed SARS-CoV2 vaccines, viral vectors, and CRISPR gene editing.

Those differences help explain why the two governments are building different walls. Beijing’s proposal shields cell and gene therapy from outside entities, areas where they have a demonstrated or aspirational determination to lead the world. Platforms must remain domiciled in China while individual products can be marketed abroad. That is a coherent industrial strategy, and it is paying off well. Chinese financial regulators report that foreign deals for Chinese biotech assets reached $120 billion through August 2026, up more than a third from the year before.

Washington’s proposal works differently. The Treasury Department proposal prevents American investors from punting on a piece of Chinese biotech and yet still allows American companies to pay for Chinese molecules. In areas where China now leads, the combined effect would seem at best to be a division of labor. As my co-author and I pointed out in our earlier STAT article, China increasingly invents and owns while American firms are more prone to take licenses, complete late stage development, and pay royalties.

Nonetheless, a decision to cut off scientific and/or economic engagement would seem detrimental to both nations.

Restriction is a defensive move. It does not put a single new medicine into the clinic. It treats “biotech” — which comprises drugs, devices, diagnostics, ag-tech, and many other areas — as one thing. Each of these competitive races is being run at different speeds and with entirely different players, outcomes, and pole positions.

The fundamental problem is the one described in our December 2025 article. American output of new experimental drugs has been flat since 2018. In our earlier study, China’s public sector, including universities and state-linked enterprises, contributed more than twice as many new drugs in 2024 as their American counterparts. All the while, the U.S. universities that built our lead in nucleic acids and gene therapy face shrinking federal research support as has been highlighted by STAT.

A competitor lacking fuel will lose the race even if regulators try to slow the opposition.

Three steps would accomplish more than walls ever can.

First, subject matter experts should take advantage of the public comment period the Treasury Department has opened through Dec. 7.

Those comments should press Treasury on several points. If it does impose restrictions, and it is not obvious that it should, they should be aimed narrowly at transfers of platforms and capabilities rather than at all investment. More clarity is also needed to address “NewCo” deals, in which a Chinese licensor takes a stake in a new U.S. company. Importantly, the regulator should set a date and objective criteria to review whether any new rules are working as intended.

Second, policymakers should prioritize and incentivize investment in areas where America leads or could lead. Nucleic acid and gene therapies depend on academic discovery and specialized manufacturing. Stable funding for proven models such as translational research by the National Institutes of Health, ARPA-H, and domestic manufacturing is the most obvious and reliable way to protect a declining margin. In cell therapy, policymakers should ask candidly why so many early trials now start in China (regulation, investment, technology, or combinations thereof), and how we might alleviate domestic hurdles.

Third, Washington should measure the race in a more nuanced way, such as by drug or disease type. The totals of new experimental drugs, such as those we have previously emphasized, can hide more meaningful long-term outcomes, such as FDA approvals as well as market and public health improvements. Federal agencies could start by tracking first-in-human trials by drug type and sponsor country. As this will take time, it should become a long-term indicator, ignoring annual variations. Policy aimed at the aggregate and/or based solely on short term measures will miss key details.

Walls are what you construct when you think you are under attack or are losing. In the technologies that will define the next generation of medicines, from RNA drugs to gene editing, American institutions still lead. The biggest threat does not come from abroad but from changes in domestic policy, such as cutting biomedical research. Our current lead in these fields was built with reliable investments by the public and private sectors, not barriers.

Michael S. Kinch is a professor of pharmacology at Stony Brook University and the author of six books on pharmaceutical innovation.

#5444. Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

An international research team has developed a new technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease. In experiments involving mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms, the approach significantly improved movement problems without requiring permanently implanted electrodes.

The technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain. When exposed to an external magnetic field, these particles generate tiny forces that activate nearby nerve cells. Unlike conventional brain stimulation treatments, which rely on surgically implanted electrodes, the new approach uses magnetic forces to influence brain activity. The findings, published in Advanced Science, come from researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), RWTH Aachen, and the Universities of Maastricht (the Netherlands) and Leuven (Belgium).

Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants

Parkinson's disease develops as brain cells responsible for producing dopamine gradually break down. Dopamine is a chemical messenger that plays a vital role in controlling movement. As its levels decline, communication within the brain's movement circuits becomes disrupted, contributing to tremors and other motor difficulties.

For some patients, deep brain stimulation can help control these symptoms. This treatment uses a device known as a brain pacemaker, which is implanted beneath the collarbone and connected to electrodes placed deep inside the brain. The electrodes deliver electrical stimulation to a region called the subthalamic nucleus (STN for short), helping to modify abnormal activity in the brain circuits responsible for movement.

Although this treatment can provide substantial relief, it requires a complex surgical procedure and does not work for everyone.

"The procedure is relatively complex, however, and not always successful," explains Prof. Dr. Danijela Gregurec from the Department of Chemistry and Pharmacy at FAU. "This puts many Parkinson's patients off, and not all patients are suitable candidates for one of these pacemakers."

The researchers believe magnetic stimulation could eventually provide another option, allowing doctors to influence the same deep brain structures without leaving electrodes permanently implanted.

How Tiny Magnetic Particles Stimulate Brain Cells

The new technology takes advantage of the ability of certain nerve cells to detect physical pressure and mechanical forces.

"We use magnetic nanoparticles that we implant in the brain," Gregurec explains. "They have a special shape and a magnetic structure. They were developed in order to transform magnetic fields into tiny mechanical forces."

Rather than sending electrical pulses directly into the brain, the technique uses these particles to produce extremely small physical movements when a magnetic field is applied.

"The traditional method establishes an electrical connection to the brain," she says. "In contrast, we use the neurons' natural mechanosensors to influence regions deep within the brain."

The process works by gently changing the shape of nearby nerve cell membranes. Imagine pressing a finger against an inflated balloon and creating a small indentation in its surface. The magnetic particles produce a similar effect on a microscopic scale.

This slight deformation opens specialized channels in the cell membrane that respond to mechanical pressure. Once opened, these channels allow electrically charged particles called ions to enter the nerve cells, changing their electrical activity and providing a way to stimulate the targeted brain circuits.

Magnetic Brain Stimulation Improves Movement in Mice

To investigate whether the technology could relieve Parkinson's symptoms, the international research team conducted experiments using mice with damage to the same types of dopamine-producing nerve cells affected by the disease in humans. This damage caused movement difficulties resembling those seen in Parkinson's patients.

"Together with our partners from Maastricht, we injected magnetic nanoparticles developed here at FAU into the animals' subthalamic nucleus," Gregurec explains. "That is the very region in the brain that is also an important target for conventional deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease."

The researchers used precise stereotactic injection techniques to deliver the particles to the intended location. These methods rely on carefully calculated three-dimensional coordinates to guide instruments into specific brain structures. Accurate placement was particularly important because the treatment needed to affect the correct neural circuits involved in movement.

After the particles were positioned, the researchers applied an external magnetic field. The results were encouraging: the mice showed significant improvements in their movement deficits.

"The effect is roughly equivalent to what we would have expected after implanting a brain pacemaker," says Gregurec.

The findings suggest that magnetic nanoparticles could provide a different way to achieve some of the benefits of conventional deep brain stimulation, without the need for permanently implanted electrodes.

Could Future Parkinson's Treatments Use Magnetic Headbands?

Another encouraging finding involved how the brain responded to the implanted particles over time. The magnetic nanoparticles remained in place throughout an observation period lasting several months, and the researchers found no signs of inflammation. This suggests that the particles were well tolerated during the experiments.

However, delivering the particles still required an injection directly into the brain. Gregurec and her colleagues are now investigating ways to make the procedure even less invasive.

One possibility is to develop particles that could be injected into the bloodstream and then travel into the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier. This protective boundary normally prevents many substances circulating in the blood from entering brain tissue. Finding a way to deliver the particles across it could eliminate the need for direct brain injections.

The researchers are also exploring compact wearable devices capable of generating the magnetic fields needed for stimulation. One possibility is a headband that patients could put on themselves, potentially making treatment more convenient and adjustable.

These ideas remain at an early stage, and the researchers expect that several more years of development will be needed before the technology could be considered for clinical use.

"Nevertheless, we are convinced that the new method has enormous potential," Gregurec states. "It is not only considerably simpler and cheaper than a conventional brain pacemaker, it is probably also more flexible. Adjusting the parameters of the magnetic field would allow us to control the nanoparticles more accurately."

Beyond its potential medical applications, the technology could also become a valuable scientific tool. By allowing researchers to stimulate nerve cells through carefully controlled mechanical forces, it offers a new way to explore how physical changes at the cellular level influence brain activity.

Although the treatment has so far been demonstrated only in animals, its ability to improve movement without permanently implanted electrodes represents a promising step toward new approaches to Parkinson's disease and brain stimulation.

#5443. Fewer choices available to enrollees on ACA exchanges: RWJF

Fewer choices available to enrollees on ACA exchanges: RWJF" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The number of regions where patients have limited choices for Affordable Care Act plans is on the rise, according to a new analysis.

The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation report found that for the 2027 plan year, there are more than 200 counties in which there is only one insurer available, and close to 1,000 where there are just two plans available for consumers to choose from.

This makes for an increase of 50% from the 2026 plan year, with more than a third of counties having limited options on the ACA's marketplaces for 2027.

Most states (39) will have at least one county where plan choices are limited for enrollees. For about half of these states, this is the norm and aligns with 2026, but for the rest, this marks a significant shift, the RWJF researchers wrote in the report.

"For the individual market as a whole, the decline in participation is sobering but not a fatal blow," per the report. "The presence of federal and some state subsidies provides an important backstop that will likely prevent a complete meltdown."

"Yet the prospect of a growing number of counties with little insurer participation is grim, and likely will not bode well for premium increases, morbidity or enrollment going forward," according to the report.

The foundation cites a recent analysis from Wakely that found the individual market declined by 16% in the first six months of 2026. The end of the enhanced premium tax credits, cost pressures and growing administrative burdens are likely to contribute to worsening trends in this space.

For instance, ACA marketplace exits from Cigna, CareSource and Medica are having a significant impact in Iowa and Indiana for the coming plan year, the researchers found. In the latter case, most Indiana counties have two or fewer plan choices.

However, there are some bright spots, RWJF researchers wrote. There are certain insurers participating in the exchanges who have beefed up their footprints, and there is a smattering of new entrants. Oscar Health, for example, is planning the largest growth, entering a new state and adding new counties in some of the states it already serves.

Some insurers, like Centene and UnitedHealthcare, are making strategic exits in some markets while entering others, for a neutral impact on their footprints overall.

Insurers like Antidote Health and Peak Health are also entering new regions—even if on a limited basis in some cases—which can help staunch the bleeding.

Blue Cross Blue Shield plans also often play a key role in limited markets, as in close to 80% of counties with a single insurer, that payer is a Blues plan. In addition, in 12% of counties, the single insurer is Elevance Health, which operates plans as Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield.

"This suggests that were it not for the somewhat unique role of Blues plans as a backstop, the threat of a bare county might be higher," per the report. "Single-state Blues, in particular, are under social and political pressure to participate in much if not all of their state, and do not feel as free to exit unprofitable counties as are publicly traded insurers."

Waystar said Tuesday it will integrate its AI-driven revenue cycle solutions into Google Cloud’s recently announced Gemini for healthcare solution.

The company’s Health feature is expanding to desktop app, Androids and its personal AI agents—dubbed dots.

Agents are designed to work with human oversight, executives say.

“Most intake solutions are built first, and providers have to change their workflows to fit them,” Wood said. “We start with the provider. We learn how their teams and patients actually move through intake, then build the agentic solution around that, together.”

Wood continued, “That starting point shapes everything that follows, and is designed to drive faster adoption, more completed intake and real value for practices.”

Amazon Connect Health announced Nov. 17 the launch of expanded patient access capabilities through the agentic solution.

As of the date of the announcement, four new capabilities are generally available to users: appointment management, prescription management, information assistance and password reset.

The company says the expansion builds on the foundation of Amazon Connect Health, which included patient verification, patient insights, ambient documentation and more.

#5440. Cloudera launches digital sovereignty platform spanning AI and infrastructure

Cloudera Inc. today announced a digital sovereignty package that it said enables organizations to maintain control over their data, artificial intelligence models and computing infrastructure regardless of where workloads run.

Cloudera for Digital Sovereignty combines the company’s Anywhere Cloud, Open Data Lakehouse and Unified Data Fabric technologies with open-weight AI models and model customization tools from Mistral SAS, with whom Cloudera recently partnered. The integrated offering supports deployment across sovereign clouds, private data centers and fully air-gapped environments that have no connection to external networks.

“As AI becomes more autonomous and embedded in critical operations, enterprises need to know that their data, models, and infrastructure can remain under their control even as technology and regulatory requirements change,” Cloudera Chief Technology Officer Sergio Gago said in a statement.

The offering provides consistent zero-trust access controls, data lineage tracking and governance policies across deployment environments. Those capabilities are intended to help organizations address requirements imposed by the European Union’s AI Act, Digital Operational Resilience Act and Network and Information Security Directive, among other regulations.

Governance policies also extend to the enterprise data that AI agents retrieve and use in performing tasks. Mistral’s open-weight models can run alongside governed data, enabling organizations to customize models locally and execute agentic workflows without exposing sensitive information.

Cloudera’s modular hybrid cloud architecture enables users to shift computing workloads between infrastructure providers and private data centers without rewriting applications or migrating or duplicating underlying data. Organizations can also selectively apply sovereignty controls to sensitive workloads without imposing the same restrictions across their entire computing estate.

Moor Insights & Strategy Inc. Chief Analyst Patrick Moorhead said AI has raised the bar on data protection. “A company can meet every line of its sovereignty policy and still not control who accesses its data or who can turn off the models it depends on,” he said in a statement.

Cloudera said it will supplement its Mistral partnership with an ecosystem of sovereign cloud providers and implementation partners. The company is initially targeting Europe but plans to expand the partner network into other regions and regulatory jurisdictions.
