#5359. ‘DWTS’ Finalist Amber Glenn Reveals the Sweet Way She and Pasha Pashkov Bonded with Daniella Karagach and Ezra Frech at Home ‘From Day One’

All season long, the "Dancing with the Stars" judges recognized Amber Glenn's competitive nature, but now that the season has come to an end, the Olympic figure skater is proving that she has been a team player all along.

Glen came in second place in the competition dance series, with two-time Paralympian Ezra Frech taking home the coveted Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy.

And while the contestants share a spot on Team USA—for which they've both brought home gold medals—they quickly bonded in the competition as their professional dance partners, Pasha Pashkov and Daniella Karagach, are married.

When asked how she felt about the results after the finale, Glenn told Extra she "couldn't ask for a better result," and described a "triumphant feeling" as she walked away from Season 35 having earned 10s across the board in all three of her final performances.

"From day one, we all met up, had a little dinner over at their house, and we said, 'We wanna go 1-2,'" she explained to the outlet. "And we didn't specify, like, whatever happens, happens, but the fact that we came in here and we both got those perfect scores. We both did everything we could and it was truly in the hands of the people at home. I'm really proud of what we did and I'm really, really happy that Team USA took it home."

The group—who have been unofficially dubbed "Team USA and the Pashkovs" by fans and even the official U.S. Olympic and Paralmypic team all season—have been close collaborators throughout the competition.

During the Nov. 10 episode, when teams were paired off and required to compete in two-on-two dance-offs, Glenn and Pashkov and Frech and Karagach put a friendly spin on the format by switching partners mid-choreography as they performed a Rumba to "The Boy Is Mine" by Brandy and Monica.

"It felt more like a team dance than anything else," Karagach told Us magazine. "We came together ,and we had the best time sharing the dance floor, and we couldn't also not end swapping partners because I've always wanted to dance with Amber, and Ezra and Pasha secretly wanted to dance with each other. So that was fun."

The competitors-turned-pals took to social media to share plenty of heartwarming behind-the-scenes moments throughout the experience, providing a glimpse at what their down time is like between rehearsals. In one Sept. 18 post, Pashkov wrote, "We're a tightly-knit fam now."

In a post-finale interview with Deadline, Glenn described the moment she had realized Frech would win. The Plano, TX native said, "I don't know if I felt as many emotions watching a performance as I did when watching Ezra and Dani. It was like, at first, it's excitement. I'm like, 'I love that Linkin Park [song].' And then horror, fear, and like, panic.'"

The moment Glenn was referring to was the malfunction in which Frech's prosthetic fell off mid-performance. Frech and Karagach quickly communicated while dancing, allowing him to secure it into place properly and complete the routine.

"I think I gasped so loud I threw my rib out again," Glenn continued. "So then, the physical pain and just like, fear, panic, and then just awe, inspiration, something you feel in your core. I know that's a saying, but like you feel it in your gut, and it takes your breath away, and that's what it was."

Glenn said that in that moment, she "was like, 'They won.'" She even added that she "would feel bad" if she had taken home the trophy after seeing Frech and Karagach pull off "such a perfect dance" after "working so hard for it all season."

#5358. Anthropic is trying to kill traditional desktop apps with Claude-generated desktop apps

Rarely a day goes by that Anthropic PBC doesn’t announce some kind of new capability, feature or model, and today wasn’t any different. Today came the ability to use Claude to create fully functional desktop applications for Windows and Mac computers with a single prompt.

It promises to be one of its more impactful updates, fanning the flames of those who argue that artificial intelligence is ultimately destined to eat the software world.

The company said today that users can now transform what it calls “artifacts” into standalone applications that run independently of Claude and can be accessed from the desktop. Artifacts have been around for a while, and they can be almost anything, such as a simple order tracker or a meeting dashboard that pulls information from the user’s calendar and email inbox.

However, until today, artifacts were a bit tricky to access. They could be opened up only from inside Claude itself, which meant users first had to open up the chatbot, login and then find the old conversation where they originally created the artifact they want to use.

Anthropic said people are using Claude artifacts all the time for various everyday tasks, and so it makes sense to mature the concept. “If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention,” the company said.

That’s why Anthropic is making it possible for people to use artifacts to create, run and share desktop applications with Claude’s new “Install as App” feature, which is available in beta now on Windows and macOS.

In a video posted on X, Anthropic showed how straightforward it is to create a functional desktop app from a simple prompt. The user simply describes the tool they want Claude to create, click confirm and then sit back and wait for a few seconds as it slaps together the required code to bring that app to life.

You can now install Claude artifacts as desktop apps on Mac and Windows.

Ask Claude to build an artifact, click "Install as app", and open it like any other app. It can use your connectors and, if you allow it, send notifications or add a menu bar item. pic.twitter.com/8CBgqe5OKq

— ClaudeDevs (@ClaudeDevs) November 24, 2026

Because these are “real” apps, they come with their own app icons and they open in a dedicated Window, rather than running within the Claude interface. They also get the ability to send notifications to users, Anthropic said.

As an added benefit, Claude artifacts that are transformed into desktop apps will be able to use Claude and various third-party connectors, meaning that AI agents will be able to interact with them autonomously, Anthropic said. However, the company did warn that any requests made by an app to Claude will count toward their monthly credit usage, which means it could become expensive if an app is used excessively.

In a blog post Anthropic showcased a number of examples of what its internal teams have built, including a fully featured image editing app called Linnet, a file manager with a cinematic design called Phosphor, and a terminal application that integrates with Claude, which is known as Tern.

There is one major caveat to Claude artifacts-as-apps that sets them apart from traditional desktop applications. According to Anthropic, “you need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app.”

That could be a pretty big downside, for many desktop applications are designed to work even if the computer is not connected to the internet. But those who lack a Wi-Fi connection will be unable to access their Claude-generated apps, even if they’re already built and configured.

#5357. What Next-Gen Real Estate Leaders Are Leaving Behind and Embracing Instead

Above, from left, Eric Fite, Jack Markham, Marisela Harper, Lori Muller and Adrian Provost

“All the technology in the world doesn’t matter unless it makes a fundamental impact on the relationship with the client, the way we serve them. That’s our true north.”

That was the sentiment summed up by Eric Fite, COO of CENTURY 21 Judge Fite Company in Dallas/Fort Worth, when moderating a recent panel of up-and-coming brokerage leaders about what old ways they are leaving behind and what innovative new approaches they are bringing to the fore.

AI and technology and how they can best be used dominated the discussion, but panelists also shared some of the ways they are reimagining traditional business practices to support their agents in the session titled, “Next-Gen Leaders and Their Powerful New Approach to Business,” held this past October at RISMedia’s CEO Exchange in Washington, D.C.

In addition to Fite, the panel included Marisela Harper, broker/owner of ClearView Realty; Adrian Provost, CEO of ONE Terminus & LEVEL; Lori Muller, president of Fathom Realty; and Jack Markham, chief marketing officer at Inside Real Estate.

The group also shared insights into how they are positioning their tech stacks and CRMs, how they are viewing their data and data ownership and control,as well as the future of AI and how it can assist agents through automation.

“I think everybody’s realizing that the CRM is not necessarily your tech stack,” said Markham when asked what old beliefs most forward-thinking brokerages have already abandoned. “Traditionally, you would pick a CRM, and that’s where your data is; that’s who owns the workflows. But quite honestly, the smartest brokers are realizing that the tech stack is way more than your CRM.

“Most teams are running two to three CRMs. And that’s not because everybody loves using multiple CRMs. They do it because it’s a fear of loss. They do it because if I drop a tech stack, if I drop a tool, I don’t want to lose my data. And so they’re doing it as insurance. So I think most of the smart brokers today are realizing they don’t need more tools in the tech stack. They don’t need another tool, another app. What they need is something to absorb the tech stack, something that’s going to empower their data so their agents think less about where they log in and more about how to drive conversations.”

Provost said he views the “tech stack,” or the set of software tools, apps and technologies a company uses, as more of a folder, and a platform as more of an operating system.

“Ultimately, what I look for is how (tech) helps close certain loops that lead to that appointment-to-close loop, and then to that close-to-repeat-and-referral-business. I think that if it’s something that isn’t touching one of those or enhancing the agent’s ability to perform, then it probably doesn’t really belong in the tech or in the platform.”

Fite then turned the conversation to AI, asking panelists how they are using it and consumer behavior data to identify when and how an agent should engage a consumer.

“With consumer behavior data, that data is your opportunity,” Muller said. “It’s your opportunity to be strategic with what you’re going to do with it, how you’re going to utilize it. And then AI is the actual action step. It’s how you take action with that data to create a result.”

Markham said it’s all about control over data.

“The uncomfortable question for most brokers is, if you decided to leave your tools or your tech stack, could you take your data with you? And the answer most likely for most brokers in the industry is no,” he said. “They find out far too late that they can’t take it with them. Real ownership of data means you control that data no matter what CRM or tech tool you’re using.”

On a question about what work AI should be doing for a human, Provost said:

“I look at it from an operational standpoint. How can AI assist me and my agents in enhancing our service to our clients? And in my case, my clients being the agent. And so I think that humans need to always be in the loop. There should never be one point where they’re disconnected, but it should be streamlined, and we should be able to have AI connect components that don’t normally talk to one another so we can perform better and elevate that entire experience for whoever’s on the opposite end of it.”

Muller added that AI can help with automating transaction management, marketing solutions, social media, communication or “B- and C-level” operational tasks, while leaving more time for the most important aspect of the business—client relationships.

“No matter who tries to destroy the real estate industry, you can’t take the relational side away from the Realtor® and the consumer. AI is not going to do it. Technology’s not going to do it. That’s the most important thing we have to look at,” she said.

How does the next generation of real estate business leaders view traditional ways of supporting agents, or “loving on them,” as the panel discussed?

“We really do everything so strategically to love on the agent, down to when we built our office four years ago,” said Harper. “We built this big hub and we put our offices right where people that come in can see us. And that’s done on purpose. We have our staff completely trained to love on the agent. We also train our mentors to love on the agents. And when I say love, that’s really being intentionally present with them, spending the time to go to their weddings, go to the baby showers, attend the funerals because that’s a time when they really need just someone to be there for them.”

She added, “And one of the most important things on that contact card is the agent’s birthday. And that might seem so silly, but when I open my calendar for the day, I see whose birthday it is and that’s the first phone call I make just to call them and wish them a happy birthday. Of course, we do the birthday cards and the gift card and all of that, but the call just to wish them happy birthday, see how they’re doing, it goes over so well. They absolutely love it.”

Here are some more notable quotes from the session:

What’s most important when an agent leaves the brokerage?

Lori Muller: When an agent leaves, sometimes they leave because they think the grass is greener on the other side, and they get over there and it’s not. So I think it’s super important to have some type of exit strategy when an agent leaves and have a conversation to say, “Hey, what could we have done better? What was the situation that caused you to leave?” And it’s a teaching moment for both people. We also just recently did a comeback campaign where we called agents that have left over the last two years, and we have had almost a 25% return rate.

Are we heading toward a world where technology becomes table stakes and culture, service and execution become the real differentiators?

Jack Markham: I think you could take two people and give them the same tech stack, and what’s really going to separate them is not necessarily the tools that you’re using. It’s once you plug in your data, right? Once you plug in those relationships, once you plug in the trust, once you plug in the consumer behaviors that you’ve been tracking and the history behind that, it becomes your thumbprint. What’s unique and can’t be copied is all the history there. It’s all the relationships, it’s all the trust that becomes your thumbprint. And so that can never really be duplicated.

What’s the one move you would make over the next 12 months to better position your brokerage and your agents for where the industry is going?

Jack Markham: Figure out if you own your data. Meaning if you left today, some of your tools, could you take them with you? And if the answer is no, then I would fix that.

Marisela Harper: I would say just be super, super present because (agents) need that from you, and just show the love. And when I say show the love, I really mean truly say, “I love you.” Sometimes people might know that you love them, but they need to hear it too.

Lori Muller: Embrace your relationship with not only your technology, but your people. Longevity is in the relationship with the people; tech stack and your technology is constantly changing.

Adrian Provost: Move away from tech stacks completely and create platforms. The old days are completely over. Whatever you need, you can literally build it. And so I would move away from being so reliant on a tech stack and subscriptions and actually figure out what it is that your agents need and provide that to them.

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.

#5356. U.S. Home Prices Ticked Up 0.14% in October

U.S. home prices ticked up 0.14% month over month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis. That is the smallest increase in six months.

Prices rose 3.5% from a year earlier in October, the smallest increase since May 2026. Annual price growth has slowed for three straight months.

This is according to the Redfin Home Price Index (RHPI), which uses the repeat-sales pricing method to calculate seasonally adjusted changes in single-family home prices. The RHPI measures how sale prices of homes have changed since their previous sale—similar to the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Indices—but is reported about a month earlier. October data covers the three months ending October 31, 2026. Read the full RHPI methodology here.

Home prices continued to rise in October, but at a slower pace. Buyers gained more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records, which date back to 2013. Only three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas tracked by us were seller’s markets in October.

However, a buyer’s market doesn’t necessarily signal strong buyer’s demand. “Mortgage rates are not that volatile right now, but they’re still higher than they used to be. That’s holding back demand and putting some downward pressure on prices, which have started to fall in many parts of the country,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics research. “On a national level, we don’t think prices will fall very much.”

There’s also more supply available now, but sellers are not willing to cut prices deeply. “Many sellers are still anchored to the prices they’ve seen over the past few years, and because few sellers are under pressure to sell, that puts a floor under prices,” said Zhao.

Redfin tracks different types of home price trends. While our weekly and monthly housing market reports use the median home-sale price, which has recently shown a decline, the RHPI looks at repeat-sales prices of the same properties over time. It provides that isolates true underlying price appreciation rather than shifts in the types of homes selling, but because this is three-month moving average, it is also a slightly more “backward-looking view” according to Zhao.

Home prices rose in 30 of the 50 major U.S. metros month over month in October.

The biggest increase was in Miami, where home prices rose 1.5% month over month on a seasonally adjusted basis. It’s followed by Montgomery County, PA (1.2%), Chicago (1.1%), Pittsburgh (1.0%) and Cincinnati (0.9%).

On a year-over-year basis, prices rose most in San Francisco, up 12.7%. It’s followed by Miami (11.3%), Chicago (9.5%), West Palm Beach (8.9%) and Philadelphia (8.5%).

The biggest price decline was in Seattle (-1.2% month over month). Next come Riverside (-0.7%), Detroit (-0.6%), Las Vegas (-0.6%) and Washington, DC (-0.5%).

Prices declined year over year in six major metros, four in Texas plus Seattle and Phoenix. San Antonio had the biggest drop (-3.0%), followed by Seattle (-2.1%), Dallas (-1.3%) and Austin (-1.1%). Houston (-0.2%) and Phoenix (-0.2%) also declined.

This report is part of Redfin’s monthly Home Price Index series. See all past reports and explore the latest data in the Redfin Data Center.

#5355. The Home Audit That Could Save Homeowners Thousands—and Cost You Only $50

With housing costs skyrocketing, every little bit helps—and sometimes, there are options even longtime homeowners are unaware of.

For example, a homeowner recently turned to Reddit to vent about humidity and outdoor air entering their home. They received quotes for an energy audit ranging from $100 to $200 and asked if this service is actually worth it.

Someone from Connecticut replied saying they paid only $50 for the same type of audit, thanks to a subsidy from their electric company—and depending on your location, utility provider, and/or income, you could also qualify for a subsidized or even free energy audit.

While experts agree that a $50 assessment is less common, even paying a few hundred for one may save you thousands of dollars down the road. That's because it can uncover hidden air leaks that may contribute to higher utility bills and damaging moisture issues.

“When you seal air leaks, you may prevent water vapor inside your house from turning into liquid inside your walls. This eliminates the need for costly wood rot and mold issues that may lead to $5,000 or more in repairs and reduces wear and tear on your HVAC unit,” explains Andrew Pho, a home renovation and improvement expert at Mister Balustealing in Toronto.

Energy audits are designed to find what’s causing energy loss in your home, but they’re not all created equal.

Before booking one, confirm what it includes.

“At the very least, it should consist of a blower-door test (a blower fan is set up in a doorway to measure how much air is leaking in or out of the home), check the levels of insulation in your attic, walls, etc., and look at your HVAC system to make sure it’s running efficiently,” says Dennis Vong, founder and owner of Inland Power Wash in Orange County, CA.

Clear, written suggestions on how to improve the energy efficiency of your home are important as well.

“Additionally, you may want to ask if minor fixes like caulking and weatherstripping are included in the audit or available for an additional cost,” Vong explains.

Niki O'Brien, operations manager at Custom Exteriors in Loveland, CO, reinforces the importance of ensuring your home has proper insulation and ventilation in your attic.

“It can prevent dangerous freeze/thaw cycles that can trap moisture and lead to ice damming and interior leaks,” O’Brien says.

If your goal is to improve energy efficiency and reduce the risk of needing repairs, an energy audit is a good idea.

According to Energy Star, proper insulation and air sealing can cut your heating and cooling bills by as much as 15% on average.

“If you spend $200 a month on heating and cooling, that could mean savings of about $30 a month, or $360 a year,” Vong explains.

O’Brien has experienced the benefits of an energy audit firsthand.

“We have seen many cases, including a home we owned personally, that needed additional insulation and resulted in lower energy costs,” says O’Brien.

At the end of the day, the information you get from an energy audit will absolutely save you money in the long run.

“Whether that means getting new, energy-efficient products, adding additional weather proofing to existing systems, or repairing/replacing caulking, insulation, or creating effective ventilation, eventually it will surpass the cost of an audit,” O’Brien adds.

According to the Department of Energy, an energy audit will typically run you between $250 and $600. The good news is you may be able to get one at a subsidized rate.

“I recommend calling your gas and electric providers to see if they offer energy audits at a subsidized rate and what rebates may be available if you were to make any energy improvements to your home,” says Vong.

Aaron Christy, founder and owner of Indy Roof & Restoration in Indianapolis, says that in Indianapolis, for example, AES Indiana offers all of its customers a no-cost virtual assessment, and a free in-home assessment if you meet certain income limits.

Your state may also offer a no-cost assessment.

“In my state, Massachusetts, there’s the Mass Save Program, which provides free audits to qualifying homeowners, renters, and landlords,” explains Ted Dow, vice president of delivery at Power Home Remodeling in Boston.

While you’re waiting for an audit, you can perform your own DIY assessment.

Make sure the weatherstripping around your doors and windows isn’t falling apart, check for any dripping faucets or leaking pipes, and make sure your gutters are draining properly away from your foundation.

“Just remember that it’s best to leave the more specialized services to the pros,” adds Vong.

#5354. New-Home Sales See Welcome Shift, but Not an Overall Improvement

With housing construction continuing to face supply chain and affordability challenges, the latest data from the U.S. Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development saw new-home sales experience a welcome shift upward.

New-home sales jumped 14.2% in October to a rate of 701,000, up from a revised rate of 614,000 in September (originally 676,000). This was also up 7.5% year-over-year.

While a positive shift for the construction industry, the shift is notably due entirely to growth in the South. While all three other regions were down both month-over-month and year-over-year to varying degrees, the South was up 36.2% month-over-month and 24.7% year-over-year.

Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) assistant vice president for forecasting and analysis, noted that while any increase in new-home sales is “encouraging,” it is “too early to interpret the gain as a sustained recovery in housing demand.”

“Elevated mortgage rates and high home prices continue to limit purchasing power, and the outlook for new home sales remains sensitive to financing costs and broader economic conditions,” she continued.

Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant noted that as mortgage rates remain near a three-year high, “the new home industry is experiencing the same pullback in demand that we are seeing on the resale side.”

“While home builders can help offset some of the pain of higher rates by offering buyers rate buydowns and favorable financing, prospective buyers are cautious as we head into the end of 2026,” she continued. “Some buyers have been priced out of the market, while others are simply waiting until 2027, hoping for more favorable conditions.”

Inventory remained on the downslope, falling 1.5% month-over-month and 4.1% year-over-year to 477,000. At the current sales rate, this clocked in at an eight-month supply, down 14% from last month and 11.1% year-over-year.

Builder activity has been significantly diminished due to aforementioned market challenges, with builder confidence recently tanking to a 14-year low.

“Builders are responding with incentives and pricing adjustments, but a more sustained improvement in affordability will be important for strengthening housing demand,” noted NAHB Chairman Bill Owens.

In line with this trend, the median price for a new home slipped 0.3% month-over-month and 3.2 year-over-year to $391,300. Sturtevant noted that this was near a “five year low.”

“Traditionally, new homes command a premium over existing homes, but in October, the median price of a new home was 6% lower than the median price of an existing home,” she continued.”

Sturtevant concluded that with incentives and lower pricing on the table, “new homes continue to be an attractive option for buyers who remain in the market, particularly when builders can offer a discounted interest rate.”

She noted, though, that the issue at hand is “that there are simply fewer buyers in the market as we head into the last few weeks of the year.”

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5353. Zoom’s conversations-to-completion strategy is starting to pay off

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Zoom Communications Inc. has spent the better part of the past few years building products to become more than just the video company everyone used during the pandemic. Its fiscal third-quarter results, posted Monday, showed the strategy is working, though more work remains.

Total revenue grew 4.9%, but enterprise revenue rose 8.6%, its fastest pace in 13 quarters. Zoom raised its full-year outlook and announced its first quarterly dividend of 25 cents per share.

The acceleration should be viewed not as a one-quarter anomaly but as a manifestation of the strategy the company outlined at Zoomtopia about a month ago – moving from “conversations to completion.” That strategy gives customers a reason to buy more of Zoom and builds a competitive moat wider than most investors realize.

The concept of conversations to completion has enough merit that Microsoft used those exact words at its recent Ignite 2026 event. In fact, it held an entire session on the topic. Though having an 800-pound gorilla like Microsoft jump on a trend might seem threatening, Zoom has a significant lead and can use Microsoft’s marketing to add momentum to its current tailwind.

Nearly all work starts with a conversation: a meeting, a call, a chat thread or a customer interaction. Then everyone leaves, and the real work begins: updating the customer record, writing the follow-up and scheduling the next step. Collaboration vendors have always owned the first step, leaving the second to someone else.

Zoom wants both. “We’d like to leverage AI to transform our business from a conversation-centric vendor to a system of completions,” Chief Executive Eric Yuan said on the earnings call. He later put it more plainly: “Conversation is step 1. Step 2, AI will take over.”

His proof point was Zoom’s own sales organization, which uses ZoomMate, the company’s agentic framework. Sellers, Yuan said, “no longer log into the backend CRM system.” The agent takes over after the call ends. In enterprise software, value is shifting from where work is recorded to where it originates.

AI agents are quickly becoming a commodity, and so are the models behind them. What is scarce is context, the knowledge of what was decided, by whom, and why. Zoom sits on the richest source of it in most companies: what people actually said to one another and to customers.

“Any agent without context really cannot get work done,” Yuan said. That’s why the unified context layer Zoom showcased at Zoomtopia is central to the story. It links conversations to chats, documents and third-party systems, ensuring people and agents work from the same information.

My Notes, the company’s AI note-taker, extends that reach to third-party and in-person conversations. Yuan said it is nearing 2 million monthly active users, with one financial services firm rolling it out to 80,000 wealth advisers. Chief Financial Officer Michelle Chang added that online customers using My Notes have been associated with a 50% reduction in churn.

That is what will create a deeper competitive moat for Zoom. The more context a customer stores with Zoom, the more useful its agents become and the harder it is to leave. Zoom’s moat is not the meeting. Think of it as the memory of the meeting.

A context layer is only as good as the number of conversations it ingests, and this is where Zoom’s breadth of platforms matters. Meetings, phone, chat, contact center and now sales intelligence all feed into the same foundation, and each product gets smarter from the others.

Customers are consolidating. DSI Systems is replacing five separate products with Zoom. SolarWinds expanded its Zoom licenses while “recalibrating its Microsoft package,” according to Yuan. Enterprise net dollar expansion returned to 100%, its highest level in 11 quarters. “Strong RPO growth reflects our continued success in landing larger, longer-term multiproduct platform deals, demonstrating growing demand for our AI-first platform,” Chang said.

Customer experience is where completion gets paid for. Zoom CX recurring revenue grew in the high double digits for the seventh straight quarter, and all 10 of its largest CX deals included paid AI. More telling, Zoom said at Zoomtopia that 90% of its top 100 CX deals in the first half were with customers new to Zoom. Contact center is no longer a cross-sell. It is a front door.

Chang described the differentiation as “the ability to think about customer experience in a whole and fresh new way.” Specifically, she said, “to be able to seamlessly hand off from virtual agents to agents assisted with AI is a big winner for us.” AI-native startups have the virtual agent but not the human side. Legacy contact center vendors have the humans but not the pace of innovation. Zoom has both on one platform.

There is also an economic moat. Zoom runs most of its AI workload on its own small models and saves the expensive frontier models for harder tasks. “I fundamentally believe no single model can satisfy everything,” Yuan said. Gross margin rose even as AI usage grew, a feat that a point product reselling another company’s tokens cannot easily match.

The quarter was strong, but analyst questions revealed several concerns.

Some will read the dividend as a sign of maturity. With more than $7 billion in cash and free cash flow margins above 40%, I see a company that can fund innovation and return capital at the same time.

Although these issues came up during the call, most of the investment community remains positive about Zoom. In his note, Arun Bhatia of William Blair wrote, “Churn and downsell rates are becoming more favorable, AI usage and monetization are increasing, and adoption of new products such as Phone and Zoom CX is strong. We are encouraged by these trends and see potential for a growth uptick in the future.”

Zoom’s headline growth resembles that of a mature software vendor, but the company is in transition, so it’s important to look beyond the numbers. The underlying enterprise business is built to be a platform that uses context to drive customers toward more products and longer commitments. Investors should watch enterprise growth, net expansion and CX AI attach rates rather than the top line.

For information technology and business leaders, the lesson extends beyond Zoom. Conversation data is a strategic asset, so decide deliberately where it lives and which agents can act on it. Insist on openness so that context can feed the tools you choose. Start where completion is easy to measure, in the contact center and in sales.

That is where Zoom is proving that the conversation was never the product. The outcome is.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5352. Engel & Völkers sets sights on Aruba as brokerages add agents

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into new markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it plans to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the company. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa said in a statement.

Rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter said in a statement.

#5351. Before Buying a Tiny Home on Amazon, Make Sure You Know the ABCs of ADUs

In recent years, social media has been flooded with videos of folks who’ve purchased a tiny home or accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on Amazon.

Touting to have dropped anywhere between $8,000 to $50,000, these homeowners shared the process of just buying a house with the click of a button, along with whatever else ended up in their carts.

But the reality is, Amazon actually prohibits the sale of habitable tiny homes and prefabricated dwellings. Its Seller Central policy explicitly banned complete prefab homes, tiny house kits marketed as living spaces, modular and container homes, and other factory-built housing units.

Despite that, you’re likely to still find listings for tiny homes on the platform, which makes it even more imperative that you learn the ABCs of ADUs.

To begin with, ADUs are additional small housing structures built on a property that already has a main home or main structure. Tiny homes are usually freestanding, compact units typically under 400 square feet—sometimes on foundations or other times on wheels like an RV.

But in both cases, the structures are economical and effective ways to achieve additional living space.

"As urban populations swell and sustainability becomes a central focus, the ability to build smaller, energy-efficient homes with reduced environmental impact will be key," says Paul Dashevsky, co-CEO of Maxable, a leader in ADU planning, building, and development.

But while tiny homes and ADUs may indeed be poised to make a positive impact toward solving the housing crisis, potential buyers need to know that you can't just plop one anywhere you please. Not to mention, tiny homes ordered online will probably also require hiring a contractor to help with assembly (adding to the overall cost).

With all that in mind, let's dig in to the details you must know prior to purchasing any ADU or tiny home. Because the last thing you want is to find yourself trying to return an entire house to sender.

While it can be exciting to imagine buying a "house" for $10,000 online, it's very important to not just look at the photos and think that's what will arrive. Read the fine print and all the reviews.

"Are you buying a complete tiny house that comes fully built, transported and rolled/craned into your backyard—or are you buying a bunch of parts that need to be assembled?" asks Dashevsy. "If assembly is required, make sure you first speak to a local contractor and determine the price of assembly."

Though some of the advertisements—like this two-story foldable container home—say they only require five people to assemble it in 30-minutes, are you really going to feel confident asking a couple friends over—with the promise of pizza and beer afterward—to get the job done?

The reality is that most people—unless they're cool with an adult-sized Lego project—will need a skilled contractor to assist with a tiny home or ADU build. Dashevsky suggests looking for a licensed general contractor with ADU experience. "You can find them through referrals or on sites like GreatBuildz, Angi, or Yelp," says Dashevsky.

As for the cost, it varies according to the type of tiny home or ADU.

"A brand new ADU built on your site will greatly depend on your region and the size of the ADU, but a good range is $80,000 to $400,000," says Dashevsky, though assembling a prefab ADU may run less predicated on its complexity.

Before you buy a prefab ADU or tiny home, you must make sure that the city or county you live in allows for such dwellings on your property.

You can start by doing an Internet search for this information. Look for your city’s planning or building department. Most will have a website, and you can probably glean some information there.

However, if you're seriously in the ready-to-buy stage, it's probably wise to visit one of these offices in person for a consultation. Make sure they allow the kind of tiny home or ADU you're considering on your property. Also confirm where you’re allowed to install it. And ask about any necessary permits, building codes, and occupancy requirements in your area.

"Essentially, you want to know every single guideline they have for this structure," says Dashevsky. "The last thing you want is a tiny home you have to sell or return because your city wont allow it."

Alternatively, you can hire a local architect who is experienced in ADUs—they should know all the city/county requirements for your location.

Unless you want to live in the dark with no water, you're going to need electrical and plumbing hookups for your tiny home or ADU. But some people who purchase a dwelling online neglect to consider those details in advance.

"A tiny home won’t do you much good if it isn’t connected to electrical power, water, and sewer at the very least," notes Dashevsky.

Speak with your local building department or utility providers to understand the process and costs to tie your tiny house in to municipal services. Or, if you have your own water well and septic tank, ask a contractor how much it will run to connect to these facilities.

For those who don't fully understand what this entails, connecting utilities to a tiny house or ADU is very similar to that for a normal house.

"You dig a trench from the location of the existing utilities—water, sewer, electrical gas—and run new pipes to the location of the new unit," says Dashevsky. "A general contractor can do this for you—this is not a DIY project— and it will probably cost around $10,000 to $20,000."

If your region is prone to weather events or natural disasters, you'll want to ensure that your tiny house has been tested to withstand extreme conditions.

"Is it rated to withstand snow, sleet, winds, earthquakes, hurricanes?" says Dashevsky. "There is no point spending a lot of money that gets wiped out in the first rainy season."

What exactly are you looking for when you're assessing a tiny home or ADU for purchase? Check to see if it says it's made of fire-resistant materials or has a fire rating (the best is a Class A or 1). Also see if it lists a wind rating—the Beaufort Wind Scale is most commonly used with levels ranging from 1 (light air) to 12 (hurricane winds). Finally, look for an earthquake resistance rating (0-9, like the Richter scale) or a Seismic Building Code. All of these will help give you an idea of the quality of the unit you're considering.

If you're having the ADU or tiny home built from scratch, it's a slightly different story as your contractor will be required to make sure it's up to code.

"ADUs are built under the same guiding building code—International Residential Code (IRC)—as principal houses and don't have any less requirements for seismic/hurricane/snow or structural bracing," says Jeremy Tetreault, of Four Brothers Design + Build in Washington, D.C. "They are treated with the same level of scrutiny and energy ratings, too, so you should have nothing to worry about from a standpoint of being less equipped to withstand natural events."

Getting insurance for your ADU or tiny home can sometimes be a hassle, so this is something to consider before buying an accessory unit.

Tiny homes—especially of the DIY or prefab variety—typically don't qualify for homeowners insurance policies. However, they may qualify for RV or mobile home insurance—especially if it's a tiny home on wheels (THOW)—as long as they meet building codes. The good news with this, however, is that you can often save 50% or more over regular homeowners insurance with a tiny home.

For people who have a tiny home on their property along with another home, or who build an ADU onto an existing home, it may be possible to insure the unit under the "other structures" portion of an existing homeowners policy.

The bottom line is you should speak with an insurance broker about what it will take to insure your ADU or tiny home since that will be an additional expense.

It's easy to get sucked into the idea that an ADU or a tiny home you can purchase online is a great deal! But it's important to be realistic about all the additional costs. We already mentioned the possibility of needing to hire a contractor to help with construction—and maybe a plumber and an electrician to hook up the utilities. But there are some other hidden costs of which potential buyers should also be aware.

To begin with, do you need to lay a foundation for your tiny home? If it's on wheels, then you can probably get away without one. But for people looking for a more permanent smaller housing situation, turning it into a tiny home on foundation (THOF) will give the structure more stability.

"Unless your tiny home is on wheels, it should sit on a concrete pad or foundation made of cement," says Dashevsky. "A general contractor can do this for you but expect a ballpark cost of about $5,000 to $15,000."

Also, if you purchase a home prebuilt but don't have room to roll it into the space where you plan to put it, you may need to pay for extra equipment. For example, if you have to "crane it in" then you need to factor in the price of hiring that service as well.

"The bottom line is that you really need to know all the costs involved, which are very likely to end up being close to double the Amazon 'price,'" says Dashevsky.

However, as long as you know what to expect, ordering up a tiny home or ADU can be a prime way to create an affordable housing solution.

Kimberly Dawn Neumann is a journalist based in New York City and the author of hundreds of articles on home-related topics for major publications, including Forbes, Real Simple, and Realtor.com. For more information, visit www.KDNeumann.com or IG @dancerscribe.

#5350. ‘Momentum is the cure of all fear’: Mauricio and Alexia Umansky talk ‘Special Forces’

Jumping out of a helicopter into water below, rappelling down a 22-story building, enduring chemical warfare gas exposure — if you’ve never seen Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test, these are just a few of the tasks that must be completed.

It’s a reality TV show in which celebrities do physical challenges from the actual Special Forces selection process playbook. It’s like a competition show, but there are no eliminations, and no one gets voted off.

To leave, participants must voluntarily withdraw, be medically withdrawn by a DS (directing staff) due to injury or be dismissed for refusing a direct order. During the final test, the DS ejects those who fail the interrogation or selection test.

Season 5 is set in the Malaysian jungle. It features Candace Cameron Bure, Brandi Glanville, Oliver Hudson, Ruby Rose, George Santos, Bre Tiesi, Matt Barnes, and Mauricio and Alexia Umansky, among others.

At the time that this article was published, Alexia was still in the competition. Mauricio voluntarily withdrew after a rib injury sustained during a hand-to-hand fighting challenge with former NBA player Matt Barnes. Mauricio said the injury took two or three months to heal.

The following challenge involved gas, and Mauricio didn’t think his ribs could take it. He said he feared having a bad lung injury in the Malaysian jungle. Alexia agreed with the decision, saying the gas was the “most painful thing” she’d ever experienced in her life.

Inman spoke to Mauricio and Alexia midway through the season about the experience, the latest industry news and what’s next for The Agency.

What follows is the conversation, edited for length and clarity.

I think for me, 100 percent, the heat. I think I anticipated intense heat and intense humidity, but you don’t know what it’s like until you really feel it … It was so unbearably hot, and in our barracks that we slept in, there was no windows, and when you were inside, you actually couldn’t tell like what was even happening out there. But it was almost like … “Good, let me be locked in this metal box because the outside is crazy.”

Mauricio: I think for me, it was just the intensity of what a jungle really is. The first day we got there … when we were all showering and waiting to shower, there was a scorpion crawling on my leg, about to go in my boot, which I felt it and took it off just in the nick of time. Because if it went in my boot, it would have stung me, no question, right?

Alexia: It’s so hard to choose because literally every single thing was hard. Part of me wanted to say the car rides leading up to each challenge, because we didn’t know what was coming, and it was always so intense in the car. My heart would start pounding … the bottom line is the hardest part is just making sure that your mindset is correct [in] doing all these things and waking up each day and moving forward because that’s really what gets going is just moving forward and choosing to keep on going.

Mauricio: Yeah, I think Alexia nailed it. I mean, for me, it was really all about the little victories. The only way to survive is by looking at small victories, small steps … we used to say just make it to the next meal, just make it to the next day, just make it to tonight.

For me, the hardest part was leaving, was having to voluntarily withdraw. I did not want to have a medical withdrawal, so I didn’t want to go see the doctor and have them withdraw me.

Mauricio: Not one thing for me. What about you, Alexia?

Alexia: No. There’s nothing about this that’s easy.

Alexia: We loved everybody so much. I mean, we still talk all the time, and we still love each other so much. The words of affirmation we all told each other to this day are so special … But I think my first answer would have to be Candace [Cameron] Bure … she’s so strong, and we got looped together for a bunch of things because of our height similarities.

Mauricio: Well, I have to say that the person who surprised me the most was Alexia … the strength of her mind, her strength and what she did was extraordinary.

Alexia: Oh my god, yeah. Are you kidding me? All the time.

Alexia: Definitely thought it was pretty cool. It was an honor to be punched in the chest by DJ Tanner … I actually appreciated very much that she didn’t hold back because I just felt like I was treated like an equal, an individual.

Alexia: I’ve never punched anyone or anything … the second she threw the first punch, I knew she was so much stronger than me. But my goal was to just not fall down. I really didn’t want to fall down, so I was just trying to stay up the entire time. It felt like a fight went on for so long.

Alexia: I had zero plans on talking about that while we were there. Before we go into the course, they make you talk to some psychologists … they do ask you before the show, “What’s the worst thing that you’ve ever been through?”

And I remember thinking, like, “Are we gonna go there? … That would be so inappropriate. Everything’s in my power, and I’m not gonna go there” … Once I was finally in there, I understood why they asked … you’re stripped down to the very core of you, and you’re tired, and you’re pushing yourself, and you’re emotional, you’re exhausted … And Bre Tiesi, she got emotional, and [she said to me] ”I haven’t cried in years. I hate crying.”

It was really about discovering and repurposing the strength that I always felt that I had, but there was a time that I had felt that I had lost that.

And each night, as I was going to sleep, I just remember thinking to myself, “This is so rewarding, and this is so empowering, and this is so incredible for someone that has gone through what I have” … some people [feel like they] get their voice back. I always felt like I had my voice, but I feel like I got to discover a strength I always knew I had that someone had pushed me to question, and feeling that was just incredibly healing.

Alexia: No, not my parents. I had told two of my sisters before, and then, obviously, I told my dad on the course, and then, before the show aired, I ended up calling my mom and [sister] Portia to tell them because I obviously did not want that to be the first time they read it. And even though I spoke about it on the course, I’m still very, very afraid to tell them afterward, too.

Mauricio: It was extremely difficult … I was just proud of Alexia every single day, every single moment … hearing that story was just another revelation of her conquering and finally talking about something that I wish she never held back … I just wanted to reach out and just hug her. But by the same token, I also wanted to give her space and let her be her in that moment that she was sharing with everybody. So there was like a lot of stuff going through my mind.

There was anger toward this kid that did this … But [watching her let go of it] was beautiful to watch … from my perspective, it was like, “Do I reach over and become a dad and just give her a big hug, or do I let her go through this moment, psychologically speaking, of letting it all come out?”

And I was just proud of her all the way around.

In hindsight, I love that she was able to share that, get it off her chest with us, with everybody, with the world. I think it’s super powerful.

Yes, I live by a lot of different small philosophies. Certainty versus doubt. Momentum is the cure of all fears. All of these are the different things where you just have to move forward, right? In order to accomplish something, you kind of just have to move forward, right? … the moment that I went from being an agent to opening up a brokerage, you jump off the cliff; you hope the parachute catches.

To today … here we are in a really difficult real estate market. I mean, it is not fun out there right now whatsoever. Yet [The Agency is] still growing. We’re still putting money out there. We’re still doing things right. So yeah, to me that’s just a philosophy that I always live by.

Mauricio: I don’t know. We’ll just keep going. I really like that show Traitors. I would love to be on that show. That could be a fun one for me, so I’m putting that out into the universe.

Alexia: My dream would be to do a reality TV show with my family … We did Buying Beverly Hills, and we’ve done Real Housewives for like [16] years now. But we’ve never done something all of us together, just us, and I think that’ll be really cool.

Mauricio: I’m going to leave that one on the table. If anything, it’s for 2030. There’s still plenty of time to do that and make that decision. But I love LA, and I think I can help LA a lot. I think we live in an amazing city, and if the moment comes, and I’m set up in the right position in the business and I feel like I can actually win, I might do it. But I wouldn’t do it if I didn’t feel like I could actually win.

Mauricio: It’s an absolute mess, what’s going on in our in our in our industry right now, particularly with the listings. My take is, it’s quite simple. I think that there’s a lot of change that’s happening. I believe that it’s somewhere in the middle. Like I do everything.

I believe sellers should have choice, but I believe that we should be sharing those private listings amongst everybody — every agent, every brokerage firm, not just keeping it for themselves. I feel like there’s a lot happening right now in the industry where everybody’s really looking out for themselves: the MLSs, NAR, Compass.

Actually, Compass, I think, wants to collaborate, wants to share, but they’re in a big, big fight. But in the meantime, this Clear Cooperation Policy is what is allowing them to keep all the listings to themselves and not share them … The PLS is exactly what that was, and I still think that if Clear Cooperation Policy didn’t pass, it would have been an amazing business to have right now.

Mauricio: We are really positioned as the premier luxury brokerage firm outside of Compass right now. They’ve got Sotheby’s, they’ve got Christie’s, they’ve got all of those different brands, and we’re the only independent luxury brokerage firm out there right now.

So I’m excited to be in that position. Competitors make you better every single day … I’m excited in terms of where we sit, where we stand in a very difficult time; I’m not excited about the market. We really need to do some things to improve it. We’ve had three years of very, very difficult conditions, and it’s going to be very difficult for people to survive. And those that do survive will come out better.

I think we’re in a good position to survive, but we’ve got our work cut out for us over the next year, year and a half. But we’ll continue to grow. We’ll continue to expand, and I’m excited to just be a part of this industry. But man, it’s hard out there right now.

#5349. We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

Here’s the usual scenario: You sign up for a coaching program. You’re excited, and you should be. Everybody wants to feel a little less alone in a job you mostly do by yourself, in your car.

You didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

The reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

Nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

This isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

The veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

We do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

What would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

That work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

We haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

If you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

We’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

You aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

#5348. Mortgage Rates Dip, Offering Moderate Relief to Buyers Ahead of Thanksgiving as Fed Rate Hike Looms

Mortgage rates have pulled back this week as AI investment trade creates volatility in financial markets and Treasury yields fall back below 5%.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans dropped to 7.21% for the week ending Nov. 25, down 7 basis points from 7.28% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac. For perspective, rates averaged 6.26% one year ago.

“Mortgage rates moved back down this week, offering modest relief for prospective homebuyers heading into the Thanksgiving holiday,” says Sam Khater, Freddie Mac's chief economist.

It is all but guaranteed that the Federal Reserve will raise its benchmark rate to curb inflation at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Dec. 8.

The looming hike, combined with the persistence of the war in Iran, pushed the 10-year Treasury yield back toward 4.816% this week, putting mortgage rates on an upward trajectory once again.

The AI investment trade has created volatility in financial markets as investors try to value companies, including the Anthropic IPO, which gave the company a valuation greater than the value of every home currently listed for sale.

AI-generated wealth is already shaping consumer housing behavior, with San Francisco Bay Area buyers and those in other tech hubs leaning toward higher down payments.

Markets are currently pricing a 97.6% chance of a 25-basis-point increase next month, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Meanwhile, pending home sales fell to a record low in October, and existing-home sales hit their lowest level since 2010, as the surge in mortgage rates through mid-October took its toll on buyers and sellers.

For buyers who remain active in the market, current conditions offer some meaningful advantages, including less competition from other shoppers, inventory climbing 8.6% year over year, and sellers increasingly willing to negotiate on price.

This week, the median listing price fell 2.4% from a year ago to $400,000, according to the latest Realtor.com weekly housing market update.

"The challenge is that until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a durable downward path, affordability will remain the dominant constraint on the market," says Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith.

Your credit score plays a role when you apply for a mortgage. A credit score will determine whether you qualify for a mortgage and the interest rate you'll receive. The higher the credit score, the lower the interest rate you'll qualify for.

The credit score you need will vary depending on the type of loan. A score of 620 is a "fair" rating. However, people applying for a Federal Housing Administration loan might be able to get approved with a credit score of 500, which is considered a low score.

Homebuyers with credit scores of 740 or higher are typically considered to be in very good standing and can usually qualify for better rates, which can reduce monthly payments.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5346. Formal verification startup Sequent raises $2.2M to prove code obeys its safety rules

Formal verification startup Sequent Inc. today announced that it has raised $2.2 million in new funding to take its Alan proof platform out of early access.

Founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set. Decentralized exchange Curve Finance is its first paying customer.

Curve also figures in how Sequent got started. Chief Executive Charles Cooper, who leads development of Vyper, one of the two main programming languages for Ethereum, inadvertently introduced a flaw into the Vyper compiler in 2021. Though the bug was fixed within months, programs already running on the blockchain could not be updated, leaving older Curve pools and other projects exposed when attackers used the flaw to take more than $50 million in July 2023.

Following the incident, Ramana Kumar, now Sequent’s chief technology officer and formerly an AI safety researcher at Google DeepMind, offered to help prove the Vyper compiler correct. Kumar co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct all the way down to the instructions a computer runs.

Cooper believes the lesson reaches far beyond crypto, saying that “smart contracts taught us that anything that can be exploited will be.” Banks, governments and companies running older systems have relied on keeping their code private, according to Cooper, who said AI-powered cyberattacks are now eroding that protection.

Alan works today on Vyper smart contracts, with support for Solidity and Solana in development and general software in Rust, C, TypeScript and Python to follow.

For now, engineers using Alan write rules for their code such as “no user can withdraw more than their balance” in plain language, and the job of finding a mathematical proof is handed to AI. Nothing the AI comes up with is taken on trust, as each proof has to get through HOL4, a checker Kumar has helped build for more than a decade.

For two-coin StableSwap pools holding standard tokens, Alan was used to prove that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order. The work also found minor accounting and rounding errors, none of which breached the limit. The founders are now proving the Vyper compiler itself, since the Curve proof does not cover the compiler where the 2021 flaw sat.

Along with AI computing costs, the funding will pay for engineering, sales and marketing hires. Subscriptions to Alan start at $99 a month for individuals, with auditor plans priced at $200 a month and team plans starting at $500 a month.

Frachtis and Metaplanet Holdings OÜ co-led the pre-seed round. Metaplanet is the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic PBC’s Series A round in 2021. According to Frachtis founder Xavier Meegan, crypto is the right place to start, with “billions already at risk.”

#5345. Tech Roundup: Zillow Preview listings go live in RealScout

Can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s new monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

“Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

The time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

For real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

The money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

Debt was a big part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and said the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on new real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and new ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb plans to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the company said in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

Instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment issues, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

“Travel is aspirational,” Chesky said. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”

The announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the company’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first announced in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

Preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

“Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner said in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”

For agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.

Meghan Markle and Prince Harry are settling into life in their new home in the Cotswalds, and according to the Duchess of Sussex's wedding hairstylist, George Northwood, the grass is looking very green in the United Kingdom.

During an early fall trip to Markle's abode, Northwood said they "picked fruit and vegetables" from her garden. The stylist has recently welcomed a son, seven-month-old Elijah, "who has just started weaning" and is exploring new foods.

"She was very excited for all the new flavors he was going to enjoy from the garden," Northwood recalled. "I remember Archie being the same age when we went on tour to South Africa, so it was a lovely circular moment."

Later, the duo would head to The Park Restaurant—a New York-inspired eatery just blocks from Kensington Palace. In a blog on the eatery's website, Northwood divulged more about their catchup.

"I invited Meghan as she has just come back to the U.K. and, though we have stayed in touch via text, we hadn’t had the chance to have a proper download yet," Northwood said of their lunch date. Catching up was like old times, when we used to have dinner together when I accompanied her on royal tours around the world."

He also noted that "there is a lot of baby chat" given his recent "solo surrogacy journey," and that he's picked up plenty of "parenting tips" from the mom of two.

Northwood also shared a sweet photo of Markle smiling with his son at her home, posed beside a basket of colorful garden-picked veggies.

Although it was recently reported that the seemingly unexpected move was motivated by visa troubles for Harry—with a US government source telling Page Six "his visa expired and wasn't immediately renewed"—the couple's spokesperson denied the claim, telling Newsweek it is "entirely false."

In an October interview with GQ, Harry expressed that the decision was driven by a desire to seek out "opportunities for the family."

"Being able to put the kids in a British school has meant a lot to me," he said of Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5. "I didn't know how important it was to me.
