#5288. Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm

Amazon and New York City are fighting again.

The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post, Amazon said it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the company wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”

Amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The company also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled plans to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6

City leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company said it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in New York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

#5287. XRP Price Stalls Below $1 as XRPL Wipes Testnet and Devnet

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP price is still struggling to get back above $1, even after the Nvidia-led market bounce that happened to be just a temporary day. Now, the XRP Ledger has another headline, with developers preparing to wipe its Testnet and Devnet tomorrow following an infrastructure failure.

The reset is scheduled for November 25, between 5 and 6 PM Pacific time. Everything sitting on the two networks goes. Accounts, balances, transactions, AMMs, escrows, offers, and other ledger data will be cleared. With this going on, developers are forced to rebuild their testing environments.

XRP, meanwhile, couldn’t make much of Monday’s rebound. Ripple briefly reclaimed $1 before being pushed back down in a dead cat bounce situation.

An XRPL Testnet reset and the upgrade to XRPL 3.5 are coming up 🚨​Here’s what it actually means, what happens to the data, why traders look at past BTC/XRP price action, and what the new institutional features bring Why the reset & what gets wiped?Ripple flagged an issue in… pic.twitter.com/xhvrjtjWDs

The reset is not a routine wipe, so XRPL’s Testnet depended on a single full-history server that crashed and could not be recovered. Ripple says it is increasing storage capacity to address the problem and reduce how frequently the network needs resetting.

Developers will lose their existing setups and need to collect fresh test XRP from the faucet. Those running their own servers will also need to clear their databases and restart them after the reset.

Testnet is used to mirror Mainnet’s amendment status, while Devnet gives developers a place to experiment with proposed features. Both serve as sandboxes, meaning the reset won’t touch real XRP or live ledger activity.

A clean testing environment matters when teams are building new applications, experimenting with features, or checking integrations before they reach the live network. Losing existing test data is inconvenient, but keeping a broken full-history server running isn’t much of an option either.

Ripple says the network URLs, IDs, and validator settings will remain unchanged. Developers can reuse some addresses, but recreated AMM pools will generally have different account addresses.

With XRP struggling to find a catalyst, attention is also turning to Bitcoin Hyper, whose token launch is scheduled for November 26. The project has raised more than $33.3 million during its presale, with HYPER priced at just $0.0136877 ahead of the planned token generation event.

Its launch schedule puts token claims and trading on Thursday, followed by the network’s mainnet launch on December 3.

Bitcoin Hyper is pitching a different kind of utility, aiming to bring faster Bitcoin transactions and Solana Virtual Machine-based applications to a Bitcoin Layer 2. The planned network includes a bridge, staking, and DeFi functionality, putting its ambitions closer to an application ecosystem than a simple token launch.

With just two days left before the TGE, presale holders are approaching the point where months of buying finally meet an open market, making now a final stretch to enter at the current price.

The reset announcement comes at a less comfortable time for XRP traders. The token has been battered through November, and the bounce following Nvidia’s news offered an opportunity to recover some of those losses. But it didn’t last.

XRP briefly moved above $1, but the level quickly turned into a ceiling again. Buyers have struggled to follow through, and another failed attempt leaves the token hovering around $0.94, and it lost momentum for a sustained reversal.

The $0.90 area is now one of the levels XRP price needs to protect. A deeper drop could bring the recent lows back into view, while a clean move through $1 would give the first meaningful sign that selling pressure is easing.

XRP got a chance to ride the market higher this week and couldn’t hold the move. Until buyers can push it back above $1 without immediately giving ground, the recovery remains unfinished business.

#5286. EVE Energy Unveils Full-Scenario Energy Storage Solutions for AI Data Centers at RE+ 2026

New solutions address power needs across the source-grid, power-distribution and cabinet-side layers of AI data center infrastructure

LAS VEGAS, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As AI workloads scale, data centers are placing new demands on power infrastructure, making reliable electricity supply essential to continuous operations. At RE+ 2026, part of North America's Smart Energy Week, EVE Energy introduced a full-scenario energy storage portfolio for AI data centers (AIDC), with solutions designed to support power requirements from the source-grid side through power distribution to cabinet-level backup. The company also showcased energy storage solutions for commercial and industrial, residential and telecommunications applications, alongside emerging all-solid-state and sodium-ion battery technologies.

From the source grid to the cabinet: an integrated AIDC power architecture

During the exhibition, EVE held a dedicated AIDC product launch and presented solutions for three application layers: the green zone, or source-grid side; the gray zone, or power-distribution side; and the white zone, or cabinet side. The portfolio includes rack-level battery backup solutions and is designed to address requirements ranging from millisecond-scale load smoothing to long-duration energy management.

Source-Grid Side: High-Power Energy Storage and Frequency Regulation. On the green zone's source-grid side, EVE Energy introduced the 1P 5MWh ESS, which the company describes as the industry's first 20-foot, 5 MWh, 1P high-rate energy storage system. The system balances 5 MWh of energy capacity with 1P power capability in a standard 20-foot container. It is rated at 1P, with a peak rate of up to 1.2P, and delivers 20,000 equivalent cycles in frequency-regulation applications. System efficiency reaches 93.6%, while auxiliary power requirements are reduced by 20%, according to EVE.

The solution integrates DC, AC and EMS capabilities at the plant level. At a 100 MWh project scale, the configuration can reduce the number of cabinets by three, lower transportation costs by more than 40% and reduce land use by more than 13%. EVE reports annual system availability of 99%, along with higher returns over the system's full lifecycle.

The system is equipped with what EVE describes as the industry's first 300+ Ah dedicated frequency-regulation cell, featuring a capacity of 315 Ah and a volumetric energy density of 395 Wh/L. According to EVE, no lithium plating occurs at the cell interface under high-rate operating conditions, helping ensure cell safety and long service life.

Also on display was Mr.Giant 3.0, EVE Energy's flagship long-duration energy storage system. Following 700 days of demonstrated operation, the system achieved efficiency of more than 95.5% and a cycle count reaching 10,000 cycles. EVE says the system can deliver lifecycle benefits equivalent to an additional two years.

Power-distribution side: backup for transient loads. EVE presented its Fortron 6C/10C backup power cabinet, designed to support short-duration, high-power load events. The cabinet supports continuous discharge at up to 10C and can deliver 660 kW for five minutes. It has a 15-year design life and is compatible with uninterruptible power supply (UPS) backup systems, with support for high-voltage direct current (HVDC) applications.

The modular architecture is designed for factory pre-integration and rapid deployment. Safety provisions include a reinforced cell design, compartmentalized thermal isolation, staged overcurrent protection and coordinated fire-suppression systems. These features are intended to help protect the system while supporting fast-response backup applications.

Cabinet side: rack-level support for dynamic AI loads. EVE also introduced a rack-level energy storage system combining a battery backup unit (BBU) with a capacitor backup unit (CBU). The BBU uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) high-power cells in a high-density 3U form factor and supports discharge rates of up to 48C. The system is designed to smooth load fluctuations across a 1-millisecond-to-10-second window, while providing backup power transfer in less than 2 milliseconds.According to EVE, The LIC hybrid supercapacitor has a response time of 1 millisecond or less.

Building a full-scenario energy storage platform for AIDC

Spanning the green zone on the source-grid side, the gray zone for power distribution and the white zone at the rack level, EVE Energy's newly launched AIDC energy-storage portfolio reflects years of sustained investment, development and expertise across the company's full range of battery products. With one of the world's most comprehensive lithium battery product portfolios, EVE Energy is among the few companies capable of directly supplying both battery cells and systems across the entire AIDC power chain. The company's end-to-end capabilities extend from battery cell development through system integration.

The integrated approach is intended to simplify procurement and operations for customers. A single-source offering can reduce the number of vendor relationships and streamline purchasing and project decisions. Coordinated development of cells, BMS and system integration can also clarify accountability when issues arise. A unified technical platform and service contact are designed to reduce maintenance complexity and operations and maintenance (O&M) costs for data centers that operate around the clock.

EVE says it ranked No. 2 globally in energy-storage cell shipments in the first half of 2026. The company reports cumulative global shipments of 230 GWh and inclusion in S&P Global's Tier 1 list of energy storage system integrators. Building on its strategy of "global manufacturing, global cooperation and global service," EVE says it will continue developing grid-forming capabilities and energy storage products for the full range of AIDC applications. The company aims to become a trusted global energy partner for AI computing infrastructure, supporting reliable and lower-carbon power for the AI era.

#5285. Primax Earns Taiwan's Top 10 Sustainable Enterprises, Marks Third Consecutive Year in S&P Global Sustainability Yearbook Membership

Renewables reach 63.69% of Group electricity consumption as carbon pricing is integrated into business decisions.

TAIPEI, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Primax Electronics (TWSE: 4915) has been named one of Taiwan's Top 10 Sustainable Enterprises in the Manufacturing category and received the Gold Award for Sustainability Reporting at the 2026 Taiwan Corporate Sustainability Awards (TCSA), organized by the Taiwan Institute for Sustainable Energy (TAISE). Primax was also included in the S&P Global Sustainability Yearbook Membership 2026 for the third consecutive year. Yearbook membership recognizes companies that rank within the top 15% of their respective industries and meet additional Corporate Sustainability Assessment (CSA) score requirements.

Climate Action Integrated into Business Decisions

In 2025, renewable energy accounted for 63.69% of Group electricity consumption, while Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions decreased by 44.25% compared with the 2023 baseline supporting progress toward net-zero emissions by 2050. Since 2026, internal carbon pricing across Group operations has incorporated carbon costs into business decisions, and a dedicated carbon fund finances decarbonization projects and green product innovation, further embedding climate considerations into operational planning.

Product Design Supporting Customers' Low-Carbon Goals

In 2025, Primax completed life cycle assessments (LCAs) for 18 core product categories, providing a basis for evaluating product environmental impacts and identifying opportunities for improvement. The company is also increasing the use of recycled plastics and advancing more sustainable packaging solutions to support product carbon footprint measurement and reduction.

With expertise in audio, vision and interaction, Primax serves three key application markets: Personal & Workspace, Safety & Security, and Mobility & Robotics. The company is also developing low-power sensor modules for Edge AI applications. Together, these capabilities support customers in addressing evolving product sustainability and supply chain requirements, including the growing need for product-level environmental data.

Strengthening Disclosure and Nature Conservation

Primax references the IFRS S1 and S2 standards in its sustainability-related financial disclosures. In 2026, the company published its first integrated Climate and Nature Report, further incorporating climate- and nature-related risks and opportunities into its management approach and disclosure practices.

Beyond its business operations, Primax works with the Taitung District Agricultural Research and Extension Station on ecological restoration at Butterfly Valley in Yanping Township, Taitung, contributing to local biodiversity conservation.

"Sustainability is not only a corporate responsibility, but also a shared challenge that requires long-term commitment and action. By incorporating carbon costs into business decisions through internal carbon pricing, and embedding green design and carbon management into product development, we aim to help customers address their low-carbon transition needs with practical technologies and measurable results. This recognition affirms our ongoing commitment and encourages us to continue turning sustainability goals into concrete actions," said Jack Pan, Chairman of Primax Electronics.

Looking ahead, Primax will continue to advance net-zero emissions, green product innovation and biodiversity conservation. By combining its core technologies with sustainability management capabilities, the company will work with customers and value chain partners to build a more resilient, low-carbon supply chain and advance its long-term sustainability goals.

Primax is an Edge AI technology solution company integrating Vision, Audio, Interaction, Edge computing, and Edge AI technologies. Its AI Sensor Fusion (AISFâ¢) technology enables systems to sense, understand and interact with their surroundings in real time at the edge. Through a market-driven, technology-led and service-minded approach, supported by global resources, end-to-end delivery capabilities, Primax helps customers turn emerging technologies and product concepts into applications, guided by its vision: "Bring Experience to Life."

#5284. RBC Signals brings in $10M investment to expand strategic frontiers for satellite services

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 6:33 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 6:33 pm

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has announced a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the company’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

In August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals announced a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

The newly announced investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, said today in a news release.

“By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith said. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the company’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas said.

#5283. Voice AI startup ElevenLabs reportedly seeking new funding at $33B valuation

Artificial intelligence developer ElevenLabs Inc. is reportedly in early talks to raise capital at a $33 billion valuation.

Bloomberg today cited sources as saying that the company plans to close the round in the first quarter of 2027. According to the report, some investors are pushing for the raise to happen sooner. That hints the planned round may include a secondary sale, a transaction that enables existing investors to cash out their shares.

It’s unclear how much ElevenLabs hopes to raise or from whom. Late-stage startup investments almost always include contributions from existing backers. ElevenLabs’ most recent raise, which valued it at $22 billion, saw the participation of Nvidia Corp.’s NVentures fund, Blackrock, Wellington and several others.

ElevenLabs’ fundraising push reportedly comes amid a surge in customer demand. Its annualized revenue is said to have grown by $100 million since September, to $700 million.

Founded in 2022, ElevenLabs develops a series of AI models optimized to process audio. Companies use them to field call center inquiries, transcribe meetings, generate music and perform related tasks. It also offers a service called Productions that delivers ready-to-use audio assets.

The company debuted its newest and most capable model, Eleven v4, in late September. The algorithm’s flagship feature is its ability to tailor its speaking style to each text snippet. It does so by automatically tuning parameters such as tone and pacing.

Users can manually customize Eleven v4’s speaking style by adding instructions to scripts. They can also generate conversations with multiple synthetic speakers. A real-time version of the model, Eleven v4 Turbo, generates audio with only 150 milliseconds of latency for use cases such as customer support.

ElevenLabs offers Eleven v4 alongside more narrowly focused models. In May, it introduced an algorithm specifically optimized to dub videos. Additionally, it provides developer tools that make it easier to integrate its AI models into enterprise applications.

It’s possible ElevenLabs is raising new capital to finance more acquisitions. Earlier this month, it agreed to buy Kotoba Inc., a startup that develops audio processing models for companies in Japan. Nikkei Asia reported that the deal is worth $100 million. ElevenLabs will hire more salespeople in Japan over the next few months to grow its market presence.

A few days before the acquisition, ElevenLabs chief executive Mati Staniszewski stated that the company plans to start preparing for an initial public offering in 2028. That time frame suggests the round the software maker is currently raising could be followed by additional venture investments.

#5282. Why Is Crypto Down Today? Total Market Cap Crashes -2.5%

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Why Is Crypto Down Today? Cryptocurrency markets woke up red on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. Bitcoin slipped below the psychologically important $60,000 level, trading near $59,800–$60,500 after briefly touching levels above $64,000 the day before.

Ethereum, Solana, and most major altcoins followed lower, with the total crypto market capitalization contracting roughly 1–2% over 24 hours amid elevated liquidations and persistent selling pressure. The question on every trader’s mind is straightforward: why is crypto down today?

🚨 IS THE BOTTOM IN?Bitcoin has been through some brutal crashes before.> 84% in 2018.> 77% in 2022.> And a 56% drop from its $126K peak in 2026.So, what happened this time?The market was already loaded with leverage. When Bitcoin started falling, liquidations kicked… pic.twitter.com/ZGjuafXiyd

Crypto entered the week already wounded. Bitcoin had plunged to a multi-year low near $55,000 over the prior weekend, wiping out leveraged positions and leaving the market in extreme fear territory.

Monday brought a sharp relief rally. Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO sent the chipmaker’s shares soaring more than 30% and lifted the Nasdaq by around 7%. Risk assets broadly benefited, and Bitcoin briefly joined the party, climbing toward $64,000.

That bounce proved short-lived. By Tuesday morning, the gains had been fully erased. Bitcoin lagged the equity rebound significantly; Nvidia recovered most of its recent losses, while crypto reclaimed only a fraction of its slide. The divergence highlighted that crypto’s problems run deeper than a single day’s equity news.

Several concrete developments converged to pressure prices. First, the Nvidia-driven rally simply faded. Stock futures turned lower on Tuesday as the initial euphoria cooled.

Nasdaq-100 futures dropped around 1%, and related AI and crypto-adjacent equities gave back part of Monday’s gains. Crypto, which had been riding the coattails of the tech surge, sold off in sympathy but more sharply.

Second, institutional flows remained deeply negative. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $570M in net outflows on Monday, the fifth consecutive session of withdrawals.

BlackRock’s IBIT alone accounted for more than $500M of that figure. November’s cumulative outflows reached roughly $4.71Bn, setting a monthly record and removing a major source of structural demand that had previously supported prices.

Third, derivatives markets amplified the move. More than $800M in crypto futures positions were liquidated over the 24-hour period, more than triple the prior day’s total. Forced selling from both long and short positions created a self-reinforcing cascade as prices fell.

Broader macro factors also weighed on sentiment. Markets continue to price in a potential Federal Reserve rate hike in December, with key inflation data (PCE) due shortly.

Higher rates typically pressure non-yielding assets such as Bitcoin. Additional reports of possible new U.S. tariff measures added another layer of risk-off caution. Lingering effects from the large Binance-related hack earlier in the period further eroded confidence in the sector.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Crypto’s decline today is not the result of a single dramatic headline. Instead, it reflects a short-term relief rally that failed to overcome persistent structural headwinds.

The Nvidia news provided temporary momentum, but without positive ETF flows or a meaningful shift in monetary expectations, that momentum evaporated quickly. Leveraged traders were caught offside, and the resulting liquidations accelerated the drop.

Sentiment remains extremely cautious. The Fear & Greed Index sits deep in extreme fear, at around 10/100, and Bitcoin has still only recovered a modest portion of its November losses.

While some long-term holders and selective buyers may view current levels as attractive, the immediate market is dominated by risk reduction and profit-taking after the failed bounce.

Crypto is down today primarily because Monday’s Nvidia-fueled rally proved unsustainable. Heavy, record-setting Bitcoin ETF outflows continued to drain demand, while a surge in futures liquidations forced additional selling.

Macro uncertainty around interest rates and risk assets provided no supporting backdrop. In short, the market tested a bounce, found insufficient real buying interest, and retreated—leaving Bitcoin back below $60,000 and the broader crypto complex lower.

#5281. New home sales surge in October, but demand signals remain soft

New home sales rose 14.2% in October to a 701,000 annual rate and were up 7.5% year over year. Builder confidence in November came in at a nearly 15-year low, raising questions about whether the sales spike will hold. Stay tuned for a revision next month.  AI Summary

New home sales blipped above expectations in October, handing homebuilders a slice of better-than-worse, Thanksgiving-time, good news. However, NAHB’s November homebuilder confidence gauge had plunged to its lowest level in nearly 15 years, signaling that builders remain pessimistic about the market’s current state and foreseeable-future direction.

According to U.S. Census Bureau data, sales of newly constructed single-family homes in October came in at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 701,000, up 14.2% month-over month, and a 7.5% gain from the same month a year prior. Meanwhile, the median sales price of new homes sold in October was $391,000, down 0.3% from September and 3.2% from a year ago.

October’s better-than-forecast results may surprise many, but they come with a catch: the survey’s margin of error and data collection cycle. They could be revised downward next month.

“A downward revision to September helps explain the size of October’s 14.2% rebound, the largest monthly gain since November 2025,” First American Deputy Chief Economist Odeta Kushi said in a statement.

New home for-sale inventory also tightened, coinciding with a decline in new residential construction. The seasonally adjusted estimate of new homes for sale at the end of October was 470,000, down 1.5% from September’s 477,000, and 4.1% below the 490,000 recorded in October 2025. At the current sales rate, that represents a supply of 8.0 months, a 14% improvement from 9.3 months in September and 11.1% from 9.0 months a year earlier.

October’s sales results may be less of a bright spot than they appear, and one strong month doesn’t erase the warning signs flashing across the new home market.

Plenty of indications suggest homebuilders are working through one of the toughest housing markets in years, including homebuilder confidence at its lowest point since the tail end of the Great Financial Crisis.

For example, mortgage applications for new-home purchases fell 13.6% year over year in October, a sign that rising mortgage rates and low consumer confidence continue to weigh on demand. The existing-home market is also struggling, with the National Association of Realtors reporting that pending home sales fell to another record low in October.

NAHB also reports that, in November, homebuilders had a bleak view of current sales conditions, future sales expectations for the next six months and prospective buyer traffic.

“Persistent housing affordability challenges, including elevated home prices and mortgage rates, continue to weigh on prospective buyers and constrain demand,” Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, NAHB Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis, wrote in a note following today’s new home sales release. “Builders are using sales incentives and price adjustments to attract buyers, but affordability remains a significant obstacle to a sustained recovery in housing demand.”

A review of the latest earnings calls from 14 publicly traded homebuilders reveals that the country’s largest builders faced a challenging third quarter, with sales conditions remaining weak heading into the final months of the year, consistent with NAHB’s data.

Last quarter, only three of the public homebuilders — Smith Douglas Homes, Toll Brothers and Green Brick Partners — reported year-over-year increases in new orders. However, nearly all 14 experienced sequential declines in orders, many exceeding 20%, pointing to a further deterioration in demand.

Sales volume followed a similar trend. Only Smith Douglas Homes and LGI Homes reported year-over-year increases in homes sold,

Meanwhile, just two builders, Toll Brothers (2.4%) and Hovnanian Enterprises (0.4%), posted year-over-year increases in average sales prices. Toll’s luxury-focused buyer base is generally less sensitive to mortgage rates and economic volatility, while Hovnanian has increasingly shifted its product mix toward move-up and active-adult buyers, who tend to be more resilient to broader market pressures.

Many public homebuilders reported in October and November that buyers remain very cautious, which helped dampen sales volume and prices.

“As we moved through the quarter, our buyers became more cautious, did not feel an urgency to transact and felt more comfortable moving to the sidelines,” Century Communities Executive Chairman Dale Francescon said during an earnings call on October 28.

Paul Romanowski, President and CEO at D.R. Horton, acknowledged that October was another challenging month.

“Demand did get weaker as the quarter went on, for sure. As rates rose and as we got into October, what we’ve seen mirrors September. Traffic and sales activity are somewhat below what we’d anticipate in a typical seasonal pattern,” he said during an earnings call on October 29.

Against this backdrop, it remains unclear whether October’s sales rebound reflects a meaningful improvement in demand or a temporary spike that could show up next month as a downward revision.

“Looking ahead, the question is whether enough buyers will follow those who signed contracts in October,” Kushi said, pointing to falling mortgage applications for new homes and low homebuilder confidence. “Builders are finding ways to make the monthly payment work for some buyers, but softer buyer traffic and fewer mortgage applications point to a tough winter.”

#5280. FlagOS Global Competition S2 Concludes Successfully | From SGLang Operators to ModelBest End-to-End Inference Optimization: A Complete Record of FlagOS Cross-Chip Engineering in Practice

BEIJING, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The large-scale deployment of LLMs inevitably involves challenges at two levels: at the top is end-to-end inference efficiency, and at the bottom are operators. As model parameter counts continue to grow and inference costs become a bottleneck to deployment, the way an inference framework organizes computation, schedules memory, and manages communication determines how much throughput and latency the same hardware can deliver. Ultimately, all these system-level optimizations must be implemented through operators. High-performance operators are the foundational layer for reducing inference latency, increasing throughput, and unlocking the potential of heterogeneous computing hardware.

For AI chips with different architectures, developing high-performance, deployable operators that work across chipsâand then organizing those operators into an end-to-end, production-ready inference systemâhas long ceased to be an internal concern for any single chip company. It is now an engineering hurdle shared by AI systems developers.

The FlagOS Open Computing Global Competition (Season 2) was designed to address precisely this gap. Season 2 featured two independent tracks that complemented each other, spanning low-level operators and system-level inference. Track 1 focused on optimizing the performance of SGLang framework operators across multiple AI chips. More than 200 operators from real inference workloads were released in batches, testing participants' ability to perform deep operator-level optimization across chips. Track 2 shifted its focus to the end-to-end inference throughput of ModelBest models. Using the FlagOS inference framework and the FlagGems operator library, participants were required to perform full-stack optimization of the MiniCPM5-2B model on Iluvatar CoreX and MetaX chips, pushing the upper limit of total tokens/s.

One track went deep into operators, while the other tackled the full system stack. Together, they provided a comprehensive test of FlagOS's cross-chip capabilities. Over the four-month competition from July to November 2026, Season 2 attracted 2,025 participants worldwide, including 146 participants from outside China. A total of 72,125 submissions were received, of which 354 were valid.

The competition brought forward many development teams and individual developers whose work deserves to be documented. Those who reached the podium did not fit a single profile: they included a small industry team working on inference acceleration for video-generation models, an individual developer working alone with AI Agents, a student who persevered despite limited hardware access, and a returning veteran who had competed in both seasons and refined his methods in his spare time. They started with different resources and took different paths. The following accounts document how several of them entered the competition, the difficulties they faced, the solutions they developed, and what they gained from the experience.

I. An Experienced Industry Team: Using Controlled Measurements to Bring "Intuition" Back Down to Earth

The c2flow R&D team at Yusuan Intelligence has long worked on accelerating world-model inference. In team member Zhang Pengfei's words, its core task is to make video-generation models run faster. Operator fusion and optimization are already part of the team's day-to-day work, so when his team saw information about the competition on the FlagOS WeChat account and at WAIC, they quickly concluded that the challenges closely matched their own work. The team began preparing during the first week after registration opened.

Zhang Pengfei explained that the team's division of labor happened to cover several of the hardest parts of the competition, including setting up the Agent environment, diagnosing problems, and improving productivity with AI. Even so, the team encountered many obstacles. Zhang recalled that, during the early stages of the competition, compilation failures occurred frequently while adapting operators for Kunlunxin. Even when compilation succeeded, the computed results sometimes failed to match the reference implementation. The team later discovered that compilation did not require access to physical hardware, so it changed its process to run compilation checks locally first, eliminating environment-related issues earlier. To investigate accuracy discrepancies, the team later borrowed a Kunlunxin P800 and repeatedly validated its implementations on the actual device, significantly improving the efficiency of problem diagnosis.

A controlled experiment on Problem 144 illustrates the team's strong technical foundation. The implementation used several sophisticated techniques, including packing two 16-bit values into one 32-bit value for data movement, which intuition suggested should have been the main source of acceleration. However, after testing each change separately on the same chip, the team found that packing delivered no measurable benefit. What actually mattered was a small cache hint for reads and writes, which improved overall performance on the task by approximately 24%. To rule out measurement noise, the team alternated four submissions during the same periodâtwo with the hint and two without itâand the results within each pair matched.

This experiment changed the order in which the team evaluated optimization results. Previously, its first question had been, "Can it run faster?" Afterward, the more important question became, "Can this number be reproduced?" Zhang said the team fixed its evaluation criteria in advance: candidates that produced incorrect results would not generate performance numbers. It first established the validation system and only then allowed AI to attempt optimizations at scale.

The same approach also paid off on Task 130, the layernorm_scale_shift_gate_select01 operator challenge. The team's first submission achieved an average speedup of 4.01Ã, which appeared substantial, but it failed to meet the threshold because performance on one chip was only 0.05Ã. The team then changed strategies and wrote a dedicated implementation for each of the five chips, raising the average speedup to 11.65Ã and successfully completing a "Validated Solve." This result also points to a counterintuitive conclusion: the best solution for cross-chip optimization is often not a single universal implementation, but multiple specialized implementations for different hardware platforms under FlagOS's unified interface.

According to the team's statistics, over the course of the three-plus-month competition, c2flow achieved 114 "First Solves" among 211 challengesâthe number of operators for which it was first to produce an implementation that met the challenge requirementsâand 100 "Validated Solves"âthe number of operators that passed the judges' review and met the development requirements. All 100 validated implementations have been merged into the official FlagGems-sglang repository. Discussing future plans, Zhang said the team would extend its work from operator development to end-to-end inference optimization for both text-only and multimodal models, measuring results by end-to-end latency and throughput.

Speaking about the FlagOS technology stack, Zhang praised its greatest advantage: the FlagOS ecosystem has accumulated a large number of high-performance general-purpose operator implementations that developers can use as references. Even when AI is used to assist operator development, the experience embodied in FlagOS remains extremely important. For example, when supporting a new operator, AI can begin with implementations of similar operators in FlagGems and then adjust them based on measurements from the target chip.

II. A Developer with AI Agents: One Person, One Pipeline

Yang Zhongwu of the EvokeAgent team represents another form of participation. Yang is a graduate student in Control Science and Engineering at Nankai University, and his competition team consisted of himself and his Agent assistants. He had previously worked on operator development during an internship at BAAI. He registered this time with the thought, "Let's see whether I can take a few challenges."

Yang's competition journey followed a very clear progression. He began by using vibe coding to optimize individual operators. After completing several challenges, he started developing an automated optimization workflow. This pipeline shifted his role from "writing optimizations" to "reviewing operators and submitting them," freeing up a great deal of time and energy. But the pipeline itself also required continual patching. During his exploration, he encountered edge cases such as the compilation-cache mechanism on Huawei Ascend chips and had to update his rules to guard against them. "Everyone is using AI for optimizationâwhy should mine be better?" was the greatest challenge he felt he faced. His answer was to understand real production workflows well enough to outperform others in both process and detail.

In addition, to address limited access to computing resources, Yang mainly rented online compute powered by locally developed hardware, which helped him make it through many submission windows. As more operator pull requests appeared in the FlagGems-sglang repository, he had more optimization experience to draw on. For example, launching with .run and hard-coding a segment of PTX assembly into the code could significantly improve performance on a certain type of chip. His workflow gradually became standardized: first, generate test shapes and scripts for correctness and performance testing based on repository examples; next, optimize for large, medium, and small shapes using profiling tools together with a knowledge base; and finally, incorporate new knowledge from repository pull requests.

The impact of this experience on Yang was highly tangible. His strongest impression was that "one person using AI can already reach the level of a ten-person team."

He also offered his own interpretation of FlagOS's open-computing philosophy: cross-chip operator support is not intended to eliminate hardware differences. Instead, FlagOS's unified AI systems software stack is designed to make full use of the performance advantages of different hardware platforms, enable technical achievements to be reused across platforms, and allow developers to move from compatibility work to innovation.

III. A Veteran of Two Seasons: The Regret of Missing by Seconds, and a Knowledge Base That Grows by Itself

Like Yang Zhongwu of EvokeAgent, Zhou Chunguang, who works at Alps System Integration (Dalian) Co., Ltd., entered the competition as an individual developer. Unlike Yang, however, he had already participated in the first season of the FlagOS Open Computing Global Competition. Asked why he returned, Zhou said that, on the one hand, he wanted to continue the experience from the previous season and use the opportunity to try new technologies and tools. On the other hand, the flexible schedule allowed him to keep developing, submitting, and optimizing in spare moments outside work and daily life, making the format well suited to individual developers. In addition, the gamified leaderboard provided feedback on every attempt.

But competition for a "First Solve" was more intense than he had expected. The experience that stayed with him most strongly was finally completing the development work and submitting it, only to discover that he had missed the "First Solve" by a few seconds. It was disappointing, but it also made the competition tense and engaging. Whenever this happened, he would look back and consider where he could become more efficient in preparation for the next challenge.

Zhou's core method for this competition was a continually growing knowledge base. First, he asked AI to help him understand each problem and organize possible approaches. He then used actual submissions and result feedback to determine whether a solution was correct and whether its performance met the standard. When an attempt failed, he recorded the error, its possible causes, and effective ways to address it, allowing the next attempt to benefit from previous experience. He dynamically collected lessons from each round of challenges, then continuously revised and expanded them based on new results. The AI's ability to handle subsequent challenges improved accordingly. Rather than pursuing a dramatic breakthrough in a single round, he made every attempt leave behind a searchable asset for the next.

This method also changed his view of learning. When entering an unfamiliar technical field, it is not always necessary to wait until every piece of knowledge has been fully mastered before beginning. Instead, one can use AI to build a basic understanding, then fill in the gaps continuously through practice, validation, and review. After the competition, he plans to continue following the use of AI tools in specialized technical tasks and to explore how individual developers can learn and solve complex problems more efficiently.

His assessment of FlagOS's open-computing philosophy and cross-chip compatibility was straightforward: different hardware platforms have their own characteristics. If developers can exchange experience and validate solutions in an open software ecosystem like FlagOS, they have an opportunity to lower the barriers to compatibility work and optimization, enabling more hardware platforms and developers to participate.

IV. A Student: When Hardware Is Scarce, Make Up for It with a "To-Be-Validated List"

Compared with the other participating teams, Du Xuanzheng faced much harsher practical constraints. A student at Beihang University, he focuses on AI systems software and high-performance computing. His motivation for entering was simple: the competition offered an opportunity to practice cross-chip optimization. He wanted to test his existing programming experience on real hardware while systematically learning Triton and performance analysis.

Access to physical hardware, however, was precisely his biggest constraint. Apart from one GPU available for hands-on testing, the only other hardware he had access to was an Ascend card, leaving him unable to benchmark performance on other chips. To address this limitation, he divided the problem into two parts: for what he could verify on the GPU at his disposal, he conducted careful experiments; for chips he could not test directly, he consulted vendor documentation and open-source examples, explored potential adaptation approaches, and developed solutions pending validation. He set himself one rule: clearly distinguish measured results, evidence from documentation, and questions still awaiting validation, and never apply results from the single GPU directly to other chips.

Even when working with the GPU available to him, Du took a measured approach. For each operator, he compared different parallelization strategies and memory access patterns, aiming to test just one hypothesis at a time. He checked correctness first, repeated performance tests, and documented both successful and unsuccessful attempts. Along the way, he discovered that making code more complex does not necessarily lead to more consistent performance gains. Some approaches may seem reasonable in theory but fail to deliver the expected results in practice. He therefore became more disciplined about preserving code versions and raw results, repeating measurements for the same approach, and determining whether performance improvements were consistent. Whenever he saw a faster result, his first questions were: Why is it faster? Can the result be reproduced? He considers this habit one of the most valuable lessons he gained from the competition.

The competition also made Du's understanding of AI development more concrete. In the past, complex low-level code could initially make the barrier to entry seem very high. Now, he tries to break it down into semantics, implementation, testing, and performance, then works through each part one by one.

His experience in the FlagOS Open Computing Global Competition also gave him clearer direction for his future development. He plans to focus his studies on AI systems software and high-performance computing, strengthen his knowledge of computer architecture, parallel computing, and compiler optimization, continue developing operators, and seek opportunities to work with a wider range of real hardware.

He also remarked that the most compelling aspect of FlagOS is the ability to study different chips through open operator interfaces and the Triton development model. Existing computational semantics and algorithmic approaches can be reused, while public code allows developers to compare and understand the implementation of each backend. Compared with development around a single device, this approach encourages developers to focus on how common logic connects with backend differences and provides more concrete references when they consult documentation and analyze compatibility solutions.

This year, development teams with different backgrounds participated in the FlagOS Open Computing Global Competition (Season 2) in different ways.

Zhang Pengfei's c2flow team at Yusuan Intelligence brought the engineering discipline of an industry team, using controlled measurements to anchor every "speedup" in reproducible evidence. After the competition, it will extend these capabilities to end-to-end inference optimization. Yang Zhongwu of EvokeAgent amplified his individual productivity with an automated optimization pipeline, searching for his own place between the efficiency of "one person working like a team" and the palpable reality of employment pressure. Working with limited hardware, Du Xuanzheng used a "to-be-validated list" and experimental records to fill gaps in cross-chip assessment while clearly setting his career direction toward AI systems software. As a veteran of two seasons, Zhou Chunguang patiently turned his spare time into a knowledge base that continues to grow.

What they share is not simply that "they all won awards," but that they genuinely developed cross-chip operator optimization capabilities through this competition. This did not depend on any single talent. It emerged from repeatedly raising questions, testing judgments, and revising solutions under the combined constraints of correctness requirements, chip differences, and leaderboard pressure.

Although the FlagOS Open Computing Global Competition (Season 2) has concluded, the next batch of challenges, the next group of developers, and the next round of cross-chip challenges are already on the way. The FlagOS community's positioning of the competitionâ"advancing R&D through competition, energizing the ecosystem through competition, and cultivating talent and setting benchmarks through competition"âhas found concrete expression in the stories of these developers.

To support the large-scale deployment of different AI chips, BAAI joined with research institutions, chip companies, system vendors, and organizations working in algorithms and softwareâboth in China and abroadâto initiate and establish the FlagOS community. It now has more than 100 member organizations.

FlagOS is an open-source, cross-chip systems software stack designed for AI chips. It enables AI models to be developed once and seamlessly ported to a wide range of hardware platforms, significantly reducing migration and compatibility costs. Its core open-source projects include a large-scale operator library, a cross-chip AI compiler, a parallel training and inference framework, and a cross-chip communication library. It is committed to building an open technology ecosystem spanning the model, system, and chip layers, unlocking hardware computing potential through "develop once, migrate across chips," and breaking down ecosystem silos among the software stacks of different chips.

#5279. John Deere acquires Orchard Robotics, an AI farming startup with Seattle ties

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 7:52 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:14 am

Orchard Robotics, an agtech company using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was announced Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

The startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, said in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

“Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu said in a LinkedIn post. “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”

The startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

Orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round announced in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

The Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

#5278. Court upholds NYC rent freeze backed by Mayor Mamdani

A Manhattan judge dismissed landlords’ challenge to the Rent Guidelines Board decision to freeze rents on 1-year and 2-year stabilized renewals, a move Mayor Zohran Mamdani publicly supported. The court found a rational basis in the board record while criticizing campaign promises and a draft shared with a mayoral aide.  AI Summary

On Thanksgiving eve, Judge Brendan Lantry dismissed a landlords’ challenge to the Rent Guidelines Board’s late June decision to freeze rents. The ruling upholds the city’s first-ever freeze on both one- and two-year leases.

With the national real estate industry watching, the rent freeze became a major test of what a mayor can do to force affordability.

Owners of rent-stabilized buildings argued that Mamdani stacked the board with loyalists after promising a freeze, making the outcome predetermined. They also accused the board of following a campaign promise instead of the data on rising landlord costs. Lantry rejected both claims.

The ruling comes three weeks after an appeals court revived the city’s pied-à-terre tax rollout on second homes valued at $5 million or higher. Mamdani posted on social media that the city has billed owners of those homes more than $500 million.

That lawsuit ran parallel to the rent freeze lawsuit landlords filed in late July. It originally was in a Staten Island court but was moved to Manhattan in August at the city’s request.

The rent freeze took effect Oct. 1 while the lawsuit was pending and covers leases on more than a million apartments. The board had frozen one-year leases in 2015, 2016 and 2020.

Because the board acts in a quasi-legislative role, its orders stand if they have a rational basis, and courts may not substitute their own judgment, Lantry wrote. He found that the board’s 42-page explanatory statement showed it considered each factor the Administrative Code requires, including the industry’s economic condition and the cost of living.

Lantry said appointees who share the mayor’s views did not show collusion. He noted that “elections have consequences.”

But Lantry did not let Mamdani completely off the hook.

“Regarding Mayor Mamdani’s campaign for Mayor of New York City, the court would be remiss not to state that such comments, promises, and guarantees to freeze the rent were reckless and irresponsible,” he wrote. “The Mayor of the City of New York has no authority to unilaterally raise, ‘freeze’ or otherwise adjust the rent of stabilized units in this City – that responsibility is within the power of the Board and the Board alone.”

He called an email in which the board’s chair shared a draft of the explanatory statement with a mayoral aide before the vote “troubling.” He said it cast a “dark shadow” over the board’s independence. Without more, he wrote, the email did not justify overturning the decision under Article 78, the state law that lets courts review government agency actions.

The judge noted that petitioners agreed to end court-ordered discovery, which produced about 1,000 documents, and never sought depositions.

Lantry acknowledged the freeze could make it harder for owners to refinance or renovate. But he wrote that the legal question is not whether the policy is wise.

#5277. Mitratech Positioned as a Leader in the SPARK Matrix™: Vendor Risk Management, 2026 by QKS Group

PUNE, India, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- QKS Group announced today that it has named Mitratech as a leader in the SPARK Matrixâ¢: Vendor Risk Management, 2026.

Sahil Dhamgaye, Principal Analyst at QKS Group, states, "Mitratech has established a strong position in the Vendor Risk Management market through its comprehensive approach to third-party risk lifecycle management." "Building on its Prevalent capabilities, Mitratech provides organizations with configurable vendor onboarding and risk assessments, AI-assisted assessment workflows, and continuous monitoring of emerging third-party risks." Sahil added, "Its risk intelligence capabilities extend beyond cybersecurity to include financial exposure, breach activity, and geopolitical developments, enabling organizations to maintain broader visibility into their third-party ecosystems." Sahil continued, "Mitratech's continued investment in expanding its third-party risk management capabilities and connecting them with its broader GRC portfolio strengthens its position in addressing increasingly complex third-party risk requirements."

QKS Group defines Vendor Risk Management as the structured and systematic approach that organizations use to identify, assess, monitor, and mitigate the risks associated with third-party vendors. VRM platform protects organizations from various potential risks such as legal risk, reputational risk, financial risk, and cyber risk that can arise when engaging with third parties while ensuring compliance with relevant regulations and industry standards. The VRM platform helps organizations understand the entire risk management lifecycle of the third-party vendors having access to the organization's data while minimizing manual activities and saving operational costs using automation. The VRM lifecycle stages typically start with vendor identification and onboarding and end at vendor termination and offboarding.

Mitratech provides third-party risk management capabilities through its Mitratech Prevalent product, supporting organizations across the vendor lifecycle, from onboarding and risk assessment to continuous monitoring and remediation. The product combines configurable vendor tiering, assessment workflows, AI-assisted response capabilities, and risk intelligence to help organizations evaluate third-party exposure. Its continuous monitoring capabilities provide visibility into cybersecurity incidents, financial risks, geopolitical developments, and other emerging threats that affect vendor relationships. Mitratech further supports risk management through remediation workflows, SLA and performance tracking, analytics, and integration capabilities. Its broader GRC Global Platform and surrounding solutions provide an additional foundation for organizations seeking to connect third-party risk oversight with enterprise-wide governance and risk management processes.

The QKS Group SPARK Matrixâ¢ includes a detailed analysis of the global market dynamics, major trends, vendor landscape, and competitive positioning. The study also provides a competitive analysis and ranking of the VRM providers in the form of the SPARK Matrixâ¢. The study also provides strategic information for users to evaluate different vendor capabilities, competitive differentiation, and market positions.

"This recognition as a Leader in the SPARK Matrix for Vendor Risk Management from QKS validates our strategy of building AI-assisted workflows and continuous monitoring into the core of our third-party risk management solution, giving customers faster assessments, earlier risk detection, and more time to focus on the risks that matter most." - Jan Stappers, EVP, GRC Solutions Strategy.

Mitratech GRC is a global leader in AI-powered Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) software. Its connected platform centralises risk data, automates GRC and business continuity workflows, and strengthens oversight across frameworks and jurisdictions, helping organisations reduce risk, stay audit-ready, and respond confidently to disruption. Mitratech GRC turns compliance and resilience from operational burdens into strategic advantages.
